# Known limitations

<!-- This page is generated by `swipewalk limitations` and kept in step with the app. -->

Swipewalk finds some accessibility issues automatically. This page lists what it cannot check or may get wrong, and what to test by hand instead. Each scan report shows the entries that apply to that scan.

- **Limitation**: something Swipewalk cannot check or may get wrong.
- **Framework note**: platform or framework behavior that affects accessibility.

## All platforms · All frameworks

### Automated checks cover only part of WCAG

`partial-wcag-coverage` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** Each check tests only part of the WCAG criteria it maps to. Most WCAG 2.2 success criteria are not tested automatically at all. On Android, when the instrumentation harness ran (see "android-atf-harness"), Google's Accessibility Test Framework adds its own checks (14 in ATF 4.1.1, some overlapping Swipewalk's own rules); one of them, UnexposedTextCheck, needs text recognition the harness does not currently supply and never produces a finding. Another, TextSizeCheck, reported a finding on a physical Pixel 4a (Android 13) but not on an Android 16 emulator scanning the exact same px-sized text (NativeAndroid, 2026-09-23); the two also differ in device type, density and screen size, so which of those differences explains it hasn't been pinned down. These are partial too.
- **Impact:** A screen with no findings has not been shown to meet WCAG or any law.
- **Check manually:** Test every screen with a screen reader, keyboard or switch access, and large text, against the full WCAG 2.2 A/AA list.

### Only some US states and other countries are mapped, and store guidance is informational

`jurisdiction-mapping-partial` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** docs/standards.md lists the US state and other-country standards Swipewalk has mapped (each shown with only its name, what it references, what it applies to, and links to its official source and the version-specific WCAG spec, an archived copy when one exists, and the date it was checked); reports include all of them by default. Several researched jurisdictions have no id at all: their own primary source isn't confirmed yet (for example Mississippi, Arkansas and Kentucky), their instrument doesn't reference WCAG 2.x (for example Rhode Island and Vermont's WCAG 1.0 policies), their own scope reaches websites only (for example Ontario, Idaho, Iowa, and California's and New Jersey's website/school-only duties), it isn't in force yet (Canada's mobile-app ICT Standard duty), or no requirement was found -- docs/standards.md lists each one with its reason. Apple and Google Play accessibility guidance is likewise informational ("also relevant to"/"related to"), never a claim about passing store review, and each only appears for the platform it applies to.
- **Impact:** A report's "Laws and standards" table and each issue's "Relevant to …" line include only mapped standards; jurisdictions researched but not mapped (docs/standards.md, "Not mapped") never appear in a report, and a jurisdiction not in docs/standards.md at all hasn't been mapped.
- **Check manually:** Run `swipewalk standards` (or read docs/standards.md) for the mapped list and the jurisdictions researched but not mapped, with the reason for each, and check who each law applies to.
- **Planned:** More jurisdictions confirmed and mapped as their primary sources are read.

### Only screens that were shown are scanned

`current-screen-only` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** scan covers the one screen visible when it runs; record mode covers the screens you navigate to. Screens, dialogs, menus, error messages, empty and loading states that were never shown are not scanned. The report lists every screen that was scanned.
- **Impact:** Issues on screens that were not scanned are missed.
- **Check manually:** List the app's screens and states (pass them to record --expect to see which were missed), and scan or manually test each one.
- **Planned:** Automatic navigation through apps

### Loading indicators aren't always recognized correctly

`auto-scan-unstable-screen` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** With `--auto` (or the desktop app's "Scan automatically when the screen changes"), a screen showing the platform's own loading spinner or progress bar is not captured while it's showing, and a one-time notice appears if it's still showing after about 30 seconds. A screen that shows it's loading only with plain text ("Loading…"), a skeleton/placeholder layout, or a custom-drawn spinner isn't recognized as loading, so it can still be captured before the real content appears. The reverse also happens: any progress bar the platform reports, including one that shows a fixed amount rather than loading (a step indicator, a storage-used bar), is treated as loading, so that screen is never captured automatically -- press Scan this screen now (Enter) for it. Separately, a screen whose content keeps rewriting itself once loaded (for example a banner that rotates its text, or a clock showing seconds) is captured once its controls have stayed the same for about 6 seconds, rather than never being captured at all; the report says when a capture happened this way.
- **Impact:** A screen behind a custom loading indicator can be scanned before its real content is ready; a screen with a permanent progress bar (a step indicator, a storage bar) is never captured automatically; and a screen captured while its text was still changing may reflect a moment mid-update, which the report marks.
- **Check manually:** Press Scan this screen now (Enter) rather than relying on automatic capture for a screen with a custom loading indicator, or one with a progress bar that never finishes loading.
- **Planned:** Recognizing more loading patterns (skeleton layouts, a "Loading" text label, a custom-drawn spinner) as not yet settled, and telling a determinate progress bar (a step indicator, a storage bar) apart from a loading one.

### Screen-reader output is predicted, not recorded

`predicted-screen-reader` · Limitation · ScreenReader

- **What:** The transcript and swipe order are predicted from the accessibility tree using the screen reader's usual rules; the real screen reader was not running. Android: pass --screen-reader to have Swipewalk drive TalkBack itself and read back exactly what it said, compared against the prediction (off by default -- costs roughly 1-2 seconds per element; see "android-screen-reader-capture"). iOS: pass --screen-reader to scan and record to have Swipewalk walk Xcode's Accessibility Inspector instead -- VoiceOver itself is never turned on, and this needs a person present for a one-time permission-and-setup step (see "ios-inspector-walk-capture"). Without --screen-reader on either platform, or with it declined or unavailable, the transcript stays predicted only.
- **Impact:** Without real evidence, wording and order can differ from what a real screen reader would say, for example with custom accessibility actions, grouping or focus changes.
- **Check manually:** Swipe through the screen with TalkBack, VoiceOver or Narrator and compare with the predicted transcript.
- **Planned:** Screen-reader testing

### Behavior over time is not checked

`no-interaction-checks` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** Scans are a snapshot. Announcements of status messages, focus movement after actions, timeouts, animations and gestures are not tested.
- **Impact:** Issues under 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA), 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable and 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (A), 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (A), 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures and 2.5.2 Pointer Cancellation (A), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA), 2.4.3 Focus Order (A) and 3.3.1 Error Identification (A) are not detected.
- **Check manually:** Complete key tasks with a screen reader: submit forms, trigger errors, and check that changes are announced and focus lands sensibly.

### Contrast is estimated from screenshot pixels

`contrast-from-pixels` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `text-contrast`, `icon-contrast`

- **What:** Text and background colors are estimated from the screenshot inside each text element. Anti-aliasing, gradients, transparency and text over images can skew the estimate. Text size cannot be read, so values between 3:1 and 4.5:1 need review against 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (AA). The same kind of pixel-based estimate is used for icon-only interactive controls on iOS (icon-contrast rule); on Android, Google's ATF ImageContrastCheck estimates icon contrast from pixels too, with its own separate method, not Swipewalk's. Focus indicators and non-icon component borders are not checked on either platform.
- **Impact:** Possible false positives or misses on text or icons over images or gradients. Focus indicators and non-icon component borders (1.4.11) are not checked.
- **Check manually:** Check flagged and image-backed text or icons with a color picker, and check focus indicators and input borders for 3:1 contrast.

### Decorative and informative images look the same

`decorative-images` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `missing-name`

- **What:** The accessibility trees used do not say whether an image was hidden on purpose, so every image without a text alternative is listed for review, including decorative ones.
- **Impact:** Decorative images appear under Needs review even when they are correctly hidden.
- **Check manually:** For each listed image, decide whether it conveys information. If it does, it needs a description.

### Images inside a named control or row are not listed

`images-in-named-rows` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `missing-name`

- **What:** An image inside a control or row that screen readers read as one element with a name (for example a menu row) is not reported separately, because screen readers announce the row's name instead.
- **Impact:** An icon that conveys information not in the row's name, such as a warning or status icon, is not flagged.
- **Check manually:** In lists and menus, check with a screen reader that icons carrying meaning are part of what is announced.

### Identifier-like names are found by pattern

`identifier-heuristic` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `identifier-name`

- **What:** Names are flagged when they look like code (snake_case, prefixes like btn/img, or equal to the AutomationId). Meaningless names that look like words are not caught.
- **Impact:** Names such as "Button 3" or "Image" are not flagged; unusual real words with underscores might be.
- **Check manually:** Read the predicted transcript: every name should describe the element's purpose.

### Input-purpose candidates are found by keyword, not by a declared hint

`input-purpose-heuristic` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `input-purpose`

- **What:** Swipewalk flags a text field as a WCAG 1.3.5 candidate only when its label, hint or identifier text matches a small, specific set of phrases (for example "first name", "email", "street address") -- not the bare word "name" alone, which is too common on non-personal fields ("file name", "team name"). Neither Android's accessibility tree (uiautomator dump or the instrumentation harness) nor iOS's XCUITest exposes whether the app actually declared an autofill/content-type hint for a field (Android autofillHints, iOS textContentType), so the check can never confirm one either way -- only guess the purpose from visible text.
- **Impact:** Personal-data fields with a generic or unmatched label (for example a bare "Name" field, or one named only by an icon) are not flagged. A flagged field may already correctly declare its purpose; an unflagged field may not.
- **Check manually:** Check every field that collects personal information -- flagged or not -- for a declared autofill/content-type hint in the app's source.

### Only the spacing exception of 2.5.8 is evaluated automatically; the inline exception is only suggested for review

`target-size-exceptions` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `target-size`

- **What:** Small targets are checked against the 24×24 minimum and the spacing exception. The inline exception ("the target is in a sentence or its size is otherwise constrained by the line-height of non-target text") is never granted automatically: the tree has no concept of a sentence or paragraph, so Swipewalk cannot tell a target that is genuinely inline in running text from one that merely sits next to an unrelated text label. When a target whose whole tap area is plain text with no separate button styling (Android a clickable TextView; iOS an XCUITest "link" element or a button with no accessibility label of its own wrapping one matching-bounds text child) sits beside a sibling carrying non-target text on the same visual line, and the spacing exception does not already explain why there is no WCAG issue, Swipewalk reports needs-review instead of a WCAG issue, so a person confirms whether it is really inline. The equivalent-control, user-agent and essential exceptions are not evaluated at all. dp and pt are treated as CSS pixels (an approximation).
- **Impact:** A short text-styled control next to an unrelated text label (for example a checkbox's own label next to a separate link) is marked needs-review even when it is not really in a sentence with that text, so it is not counted as a confirmed WCAG issue until a person checks it. A genuine inline link the tree shows differently -- a link inside a UITextView's paragraph, or an Android ClickableSpan -- is not recognized by this check and is evaluated as if no exception applied. A tap-gesture label that a platform doesn't expose as a target at all (for example a MAUI Label with a tap gesture on Android, which uiautomator never reports as clickable -- as in BuggyApp's planted bug B10) can't be evaluated by this rule in the first place, on that platform. A flagged target may also still be acceptable under one of the other, unevaluated exceptions.
- **Check manually:** For each flagged target, check whether an equivalent larger control exists on the same screen, the target is inline in text, it is a platform-default control whose size the app did not set, or it must be that size to work (essential).

### Findings are mapped to WCAG 2.2; laws reference different WCAG versions

`wcag-version` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** Each finding cites WCAG 2.2 criteria and is labelled with the standards whose WCAG version and level include it (for example ADA Title II references WCAG 2.1 AA, Section 508 WCAG 2.0 AA). WCAG 2.2 adds criteria that are not in 2.0 or 2.1, such as 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), and removes 4.1.1 Parsing. Section 508 and EN 301 549 apply WCAG to non-web software with some criteria excluded or reworded; the mapping uses version, level and the known exclusions only.
- **Impact:** "Relevant to" is a mapping, not a legal conclusion. Standards' own exceptions are not evaluated; requirements beyond WCAG are listed with a per-run status in the report's Beyond WCAG section (see "beyond-wcag-clauses"), most needing a person; 4.1.1 Parsing is not assessed.
- **Check manually:** Confirm which standard, WCAG version and level your contract or regulation requires (see docs/standards.md), and scan with --standard to focus the report on it.

### Requirements beyond WCAG are listed; few are partly checked by automation

`beyond-wcag-clauses` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** Section 508 (Chapters 5 and 6) and EN 301 549 (clauses 5, 6, 7 and 11) add requirements beyond what they reference from WCAG. The report's "Beyond WCAG" section lists each clause with an honest status: partly checked by automation (reusing an existing signal, for example the large-text and dark/light rescans, or the accessible names Swipewalk already reads for WCAG 4.1.2 -- carrying no finding count of its own; those stay under the WCAG criterion), needing a guided check with 1-3 steps, or not testable by Swipewalk (documentation, support services or platform/OS behaviour). Clauses that only apply when the app has a specific feature (two-way voice calling, video, biometric sign-in, content authoring) are reported as "not tested": Swipewalk does not yet detect whether a scanned app actually has that feature, so it never assumes a conditional clause doesn't apply. An always-applicable clause whose evidence (the large-text or dark/light rescan) didn't run this time is also "not tested", naming what to run.
- **Impact:** A conditional clause always needs a person to first decide whether it applies at all, then check it by hand. "Not tested" here does not mean the clause is irrelevant.
- **Check manually:** For each conditional clause in the report, decide from the app's real features whether it applies, then follow its guided steps or the standard's own text.
- **Planned:** Per-feature detection (e.g. video or call controls in the tree) so an app confirmed not to have the feature is reported as not applicable instead of not tested.

### Results reflect the rule versions listed in the report

`rule-versions` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** Rules and standards mappings are checked against specific versions of WCAG, laws and platform guidelines, listed in each report with the date the mapping was reviewed. Swipewalk does not detect changes to them automatically.
- **Impact:** After a law, standard or guideline changes, results may not reflect the new requirements until Swipewalk is updated. The HTML report warns when a mapping was last reviewed more than a year earlier.
- **Check manually:** Check the listed sources for changes before relying on results, and keep Swipewalk up to date.

### Scans use the device's current settings unless told to check the alternative too

`device-settings` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** Each scan captures the screen as the device is. `scan --appearance both` captures the screen in the device's other dark/light appearance too and runs every check on it (Android `cmd uimode night`; iOS Simulator `simctl ui appearance`; a physical iPhone through the harness driving Settings > Appearance -- skipped with a reason if the iPhone is left on Automatic, since there is then no fixed "current" appearance to switch from), restoring the device's original appearance afterward (on Android the setting is read and put back as it was: on, off, sunset to sunrise, bedtime, or a custom schedule with its start and end times (the reading and restoring are checked in unit tests against sample `cmd uimode` output; restoring a schedule has not yet been tried on a phone); if it can't be read, the check is skipped with a reason). `scan --orientation both` does the same for portrait/landscape (Android `settings put system accelerometer_rotation`/`user_rotation`; iOS through the scanning harness's `XCUIDevice.shared.orientation`, the same call for the Simulator and a physical iPhone). On Android it restores the device's exact original orientation and rotation-lock state afterward (if those settings can't be read, the orientation check is skipped with a reason); on iOS there is no way to read the original orientation back, so it rotates back to whichever of portrait/landscape the first capture showed. Without either flag, only the device's current appearance and orientation are checked.
- **Impact:** 1.4.10 Reflow is tested only partly, and on iOS only: the offscreen-unreachable rule checks the device's current orientation and text size for content pushed off-screen with no way to scroll to it, but rotation and text-zoom scenarios are not tested. Contrast is checked in both dark and light appearance only when `--appearance both` was used; otherwise only the device's current appearance is checked -- why that matters: `scan --appearance both` on Microsoft's WeatherTwentyOne sample (2026-09-23, an Android emulator and a Pixel 4a) found 5 genuine WCAG 1.4.3 contrast failures in light appearance and none in dark, on both devices, in a single run each (see docs/case-study.md). 1.3.4 Orientation is checked only when `--orientation both` was used, and even then only for review -- Swipewalk can tell whether a screen's content followed the rotation, not whether staying in one orientation is essential to it, so a flagged screen still needs a person's judgment. 1.4.4 Resize Text is tested only partly: in record mode and scan --large-text, by comparing the screen at the OS text-size setting (Android font scale 2.0, exactly the 200% 1.4.4 asks for; iOS accessibility size AX3, about 235%, beyond it), and otherwise only where Apple's audit reports it. Text that does not grow is always reported against 1.4.4 regardless of which of those two levels was tested, since it implies text can't reach 200% either way; clipping or overlap seen only on iOS at AX3 (above 200%) is reported as a platform advisory against Apple's Dynamic Type guidance instead of a WCAG finding. Other resize mechanisms are not tested.
- **Check manually:** Repeat key screens at 200% text size (and your platform's largest setting), in landscape, and in dark mode; also check any in-app text size controls. Pass --appearance both and --orientation both to check the alternative appearance and orientation automatically instead of by hand.

### Headings and structure are not checked

`no-heading-checks` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** Heading roles are not reliably exposed by the collectors yet, so missing or wrong headings and reading structure are not checked. On Android, the instrumentation harness now reads Android's own heading flag (isHeading(), API 28), but no check uses it yet; headings and reading structure are still not checked on any platform.
- **Impact:** Issues under 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (A) and 2.4.6 Headings and Labels (AA) are not detected for headings.
- **Check manually:** With a screen reader, navigate by headings and check that section titles are announced as headings.

### Some production apps limit what can be scanned

`production-builds` · Limitation · Detection

- **What:** Scanning works on release and store builds, with no source code or debug build. But apps can block screenshots (Android FLAG_SECURE on banking, password or DRM screens; the scanner reports these screens and skips pixel checks), refuse to run while automation is active (some anti-tamper protections), or draw their own UI without accessibility information (games, canvas-based UIs), leaving little to check.
- **Impact:** Contrast and close-ups are unavailable on blocked screens; protected apps may not be scannable; custom-drawn screens may show few findings even when they have many problems.
- **Check manually:** Test such screens by hand with the screen reader, and check contrast with a color picker on the device.

### The PDF export can't draw every character, and doesn't bold non-Latin text

`pdf-export-font-coverage` · Limitation · Export

- **What:** `swipewalk export --format pdf` embeds Open Sans plus fallback fonts for Devanagari, Arabic, and a subset of common-use Japanese (see THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md). Chinese text beyond that bundled Japanese subset is not covered. The subset is kana plus the ~2,225 Jōyō/Jinmeiyō kanji (common-use Japanese), not the full Chinese character set, to keep the bundled file under 1 MB instead of the ~10 MB a full CJK font would need -- a Chinese-specific character outside that list (for example "你") shows as `?` in the PDF, not the real character. Findings carry real app text and captured screen-reader speech, so a scan of a Chinese-language app can contain such characters (TalkBack capture has been verified in English, Spanish, Hindi, Arabic and Japanese, not Chinese). Any character outside all four bundled fonts' coverage (this also includes most emoji) is likewise shown as `?`. None of the three fallback fonts have a bold weight bundled, so bold text (e.g. headings) in Devanagari, Arabic or Japanese draws in the regular weight instead.
- **Impact:** A `?` in a PDF export doesn't show the real text -- for Chinese specifically, most non-Japanese-shared characters will show this way; a heading in one of these scripts looks the same weight as body text.
- **Check manually:** Check the HTML report or results.json from the same run for the exact text.
- **Planned:** Bundle a Chinese-specific font (or a larger shared CJK subset) if real reports need it, or a bold weight for the three fallback fonts.

### The PDF export doesn't shape or fully reorder Arabic text

`pdf-export-arabic-not-shaped` · Limitation · Export

- **What:** `swipewalk export --format pdf` draws Arabic letters in their isolated form (PDFsharp, the library it's built on, does not perform Arabic contextual shaping/joining) and only reorders whole runs of pure Arabic text for approximate right-to-left display -- a line mixing Arabic with Latin words or digits doesn't reorder those relative to each other. A screen reader (or any tool that reads the PDF's tagged structure) still gets the correct, original reading order via a `/ActualText` override, verified by reading the exported PDF's own structure tree back after export.
- **Impact:** Arabic text in an exported PDF is legible but doesn't look like normal Arabic typesetting, and a sighted reader may see a mixed-language line in a confusing order.
- **Check manually:** Check the HTML report or results.json from the same run for the exact text.
- **Planned:** Implement the parts of the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (UAX #9) and Arabic shaping this needs, if demand justifies it.

### The auto-updating-content check is a heuristic (it can miss or over-flag content), and only runs in a single-screen scan

`auto-update-detection-heuristic` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** scan --auto-update-content takes a few further captures of a screen, spaced unevenly with no input (each gap deliberately longer than the last -- see --auto-update-interval), and reports ANY gap between captures where content changed, for review against WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide. It compares accessibility trees, not screenshot pixels, so it never mistakes a blinking text-input caret for a change. Wording states only what was observed: a single changed gap is worded as one observed change, naming whether later captures looked the same again (which does not show it stopped -- content that cycles looks unchanged whenever a capture lands on the same point in its cycle) or whether that was the last capture taken (so nothing after it was observed); two or more changed gaps are worded more strongly, naming how many of the gaps changed; a value returning to one seen in an earlier capture (cycling) is called out separately as stronger evidence, since a coincidental exact repeat is less likely than two unrelated one-off changes. It's still a heuristic in both directions: it compares any element that changed in each gap, not necessarily the same element every time, so two unrelated, near-instantaneous transitions (for example a screen that loads in two visible steps) can be reported the same as a genuinely repeating element -- a returning exact value (cycling) is the one signal that rules this out, when it happens. Going the other way, a single changed gap is reported too, so a one-off transition (a spinner finishing, content finishing loading, a message disappearing) can produce a finding on its own, with no further evidence it repeats -- the wording says only what was seen, never that it's sustained. It can also still miss real auto-updating content: a carousel or ticker whose cycle length happens to divide every sampled gap evenly can look unchanged at every capture (growing, uneven gaps make this less likely than one fixed interval repeated, but do not rule it out). It also can't tell whether the changing content is shown alongside other content (WCAG 2.2.2 only applies when it is -- content that is the only thing on the screen, like a preloader, is exempt) or whether a pause/stop/hide control already exists elsewhere on the screen, so every finding needs both checked by hand. It never touches the device, unlike the appearance and orientation rescans, so it works on a physical device too -- but it runs in a single-screen scan only (the desktop app's "Also check for content that changes by itself", under More checks on New scan, or `scan --auto-update-content`); a recording doesn't offer it yet. Real regression evidence: a capture sequence from BuggyApp's Payment history screen on the iOS Simulator (2026-09-26), spaced a fixed ~12 seconds apart under the earlier design, sampled a promo banner that changes message every 2 seconds (3 messages, repeating every 6 seconds) so that only one of the two gaps landed on a different message -- the earlier two-consecutive-gaps rule reported nothing; trimmed copies of those captures' trees now produce a single-observed-change finding. The corrected, unevenly-spaced capture schedule has not yet been re-verified on a live scan.
- **Impact:** A screen with no auto-updating-content finding has not been shown to have no moving, blinking, scrolling or auto-updating content; a finding is not proof the content keeps changing (a single changed gap may be a one-off, such as content finishing loading), is shown alongside other content, or is missing a control; and the check isn't available at all outside scan.
- **Check manually:** Watch each screen for at least 10-15 seconds with no input and check any moving, blinking, scrolling or auto-updating content for a way to pause, stop or hide it.
- **Planned:** Wiring the check into record

### Fix examples for an unidentified framework, or one without an example for a check, are generic

`other-framework-fix-examples` · Limitation · FixExamples

- **What:** A screen whose framework is Unknown (no detection signal, and no --framework), or whose known framework has no example for a particular check, gets the platform's combined native example (Android code covering Views and Compose, or iOS Swift code in UIKit with causes covering both UIKit and SwiftUI) instead of a framework-specific one, and the report, tickets and exports label it "Generic example" wherever it appears (never assuming .NET MAUI). UIKit and SwiftUI in particular are not yet detected automatically from a captured tree at all (see "framework-detection-partial"), so on iOS today their own examples show only with an explicit `--framework uikit`/`--framework swiftui`.
- **Impact:** On a screen whose framework Swipewalk couldn't identify (or wasn't told), or for a check with no example for the app's framework, the code example's syntax may not match the app's own framework; the finding and the kind of fix it needs don't depend on the framework.
- **Check manually:** Pass --framework when you know the app's framework (the desktop app's App framework menu under More checks on New scan does the same -- see "framework-detection-partial"); otherwise apply the same fix with the framework's own accessibility API. When the framework is known but the check has no example for it, apply the same fix with that framework's own accessibility API.
- **Planned:** A verified iOS signal for UIKit and SwiftUI, if one is found, so their own examples show without --framework.

### Framework detection can't tell every framework apart, and some signals are unverified

`framework-detection-partial` · Limitation · Detection

- **What:** Detection reads the captured accessibility tree's own native class names (Android: FlutterView, ReactRootView, ComposeView; a WebView filling the screen on either platform) or, on iOS, the installed app bundle (Simulator, or a physical iPhone Swipewalk itself installed with --install). Two gaps: (1) iOS's XCUITest tree has no class-name field at all -- only a coarse element type, identifier and label -- so UIKit and SwiftUI cannot be told apart there, and neither can Flutter or React Native from the tree alone; those two are detected only from the app bundle, so an iOS app already installed some other way (Xcode, TestFlight, the App Store, an MDM) stays Unknown unless it's a WebView-filling hybrid-web app or --framework names it directly. (2) Flutter's and React Native's own Android class names (FlutterView, ReactRootView), and the iOS bundle markers for Flutter (Frameworks/Flutter.framework) and React Native (Frameworks/hermes.framework or main.jsbundle), are real, documented signals but not verified against a real Flutter or React Native build in this project's own testing on either platform -- unlike the MAUI markers and Android's own Jetpack Compose class name, which are confirmed; the generic Android Views bucket (no more specific class name found) is itself shown as likely too, since it's a fallback for whatever's left rather than one specific, verified class name. Uiautomator's own "class" attribute is also a name an app can set to whatever it likes (AccessibilityNodeInfo#getClassName), not necessarily the real Java class, which the Android signal can't rule out either. A detection's confidence (results.json's frameworkConfidence: "confirmed" or "likely") and its evidence are recorded so a report never overstates one it isn't sure of.
- **Impact:** A UIKit or SwiftUI app, or a Flutter/React Native app on an iOS device Swipewalk didn't install, reports as Unknown and gets generic native fix advice; any Flutter/React Native detection (Android or iOS) has not been confirmed against a real build of that framework.
- **Check manually:** Pass --framework when you know the app's framework and want its own advice (the desktop app's App framework menu, under More checks on New scan, does the same); check frameworkConfidence in results.json before treating a Likely Flutter/React Native detection as certain.
- **Planned:** A verified iOS signal for UIKit/SwiftUI/Flutter/React Native, if one is found; device verification of the Flutter/React Native class names and bundle markers.

## Android · All frameworks

### Android App Bundles need bundletool and Java, and IDE-only debug builds can't be installed from a file

`android-install-files` · Limitation · Devices

- **What:** --install takes a signed .apk (debug or release) directly, and an Android App Bundle (.aab) via Google's bundletool: it's usually found automatically (on PATH, or bundled with the installed .NET Android SDK workload), needs a Java runtime to run, and builds a set of .apks for the connected device, signed with the standard Android debug key (~/.android/debug.keystore, created by Swipewalk with keytool if it doesn't already exist, using the same standard settings Android Studio and Gradle use) unless --keystore is given -- a debug-signed build differs from your store build, for scanning only, and installing over an app already installed with a different key fails until it's uninstalled or the matching --keystore is given. .NET MAUI Debug builds that use fast deployment still cannot run on their own, in either format (detected and explained).
- **Impact:** A .aab install needs bundletool and a Java runtime present (a clear message says how to get them if not); a MAUI Debug fast-deployment build is refused either way. The app can still be scanned once installed another way.
- **Check manually:** Install bundletool (brew install bundletool, or the .NET Android SDK workload already has it, pointed at with --bundletool if it isn't found automatically) and a JRE if the message says they're missing, or build MAUI apps in Release (or with EmbedAssembliesIntoApk=true).

### The Android tree comes from uiautomator, not TalkBack

`android-uiautomator-view` · Limitation · Detection

- **What:** Elements, names and reachability are read with uiautomator dumps. The compressed dump is used to decide what TalkBack can reach, which approximates TalkBack's own rules. When the instrumentation harness ran (see "android-atf-harness"), the extra properties it adds and Google's ATF checks are read from Android's accessibility framework (AccessibilityNodeInfo, through UiAutomation) directly, the same kind of node data TalkBack itself receives, rather than a uiautomator dump -- but still not the exact node set TalkBack works from (the harness can also see views marked not important for accessibility) and without TalkBack's own filtering and grouping on top, so this does not mean the scanner sees exactly what TalkBack does.
- **Impact:** TalkBack may group, skip or name some elements differently than predicted.
- **Check manually:** Confirm unlabeled and unreachable elements with TalkBack.
- **Planned:** More automated checks on Android; screen-reader testing

### Android 14+ enlarges big text less than the font scale

`android-nonlinear-font-scaling` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `text-resize`

- **What:** From Android 14, text that is already large grows less than the font-scale setting, by design. At font scale 2.0 a large heading can grow well under 2×.
- **Impact:** Large headings may be listed under Needs review for not growing even though the platform is working as intended.
- **Check manually:** For flagged large text, check at 200% text size whether it is still readable and not clipped.

### Changing the text size can restart the screen

`android-font-scale-restart` · Limitation · Detection · rules: `text-resize`, `text-resize-navigation`

- **What:** Android restarts the current activity when the font scale changes unless the app handles that change. scan --large-text and record wait briefly for the app to return to the front, then skip the large-text check for that screen (and say why) if it shows a different screen, or never comes back to front, at the larger size. When the very first attempt at the larger size shows a different screen, a platform advisory (text-resize-navigation) is also added to the screen where Swipewalk actually saw it, flagging the lost place itself -- but only for that one screen, not for every screen skipped this way.
- **Impact:** Some screens may have no large-text check; app state (such as typed text) can be lost when the text size changes.
- **Check manually:** For screens without a large-text capture, set the system font size to 200% and check them by hand.

### Off-screen content is not detected on Android

`offscreen-unreachable-android-gap` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `offscreen-unreachable`

- **What:** offscreen-unreachable flags controls or text positioned wholly or mostly outside the visible screen at normal text size, with no scrollable ancestor that could bring them into view. It runs on iOS only: Android's uiautomator dump does not report a node's true position when part or all of it is off-screen. AOSP's AccessibilityNodeInfoDumper writes each node's bounds through getVisibleBoundsInScreen, which clips them to the screen's visible area first, and a node that is entirely off-screen is omitted from the dump altogether (see "large-text-lost-content-heuristic"). Confirmed in a saved capture of the sample app on a Pixel 4a at large text: "Pay", cut off at the bottom of that capture, has bounds ending exactly at the screen's edge (2340 px), never beyond it. On iOS, XCUITest's snapshot usually keeps an element's real frame regardless of its position (lazily-created content, such as an unrendered table/collection cell, can still be absent), which is what this rule reads instead.
- **Impact:** Every case on Android is missed: a control positioned off-screen on Android never produces a finding from this rule, however far past the edge it actually sits.
- **Check manually:** On Android, check by hand whether every control shown in the app's source or design is reachable on the actual device screen, especially near the bottom of a long, non-scrolling layout.

### Text field contents and hints can't be told apart without the Android harness

`android-edittext-text` · Limitation · ScreenReader · rules: `missing-name`

- **What:** On Android, a text field's typed value, its placeholder and some labels can all appear as the field's text. When the Android instrumentation harness ran for a capture, AccessibilityNodeInfo#getHintText() (API 26) recovers a placeholder even on a device/version whose uiautomator dump omits the "hint" attribute (seen on an Android 13 phone, not on an Android 16 emulator), so a field with a real hint gets a name and is not flagged at all. isShowingHintText() (API 26) then tells whether a field with no hint and no label is showing a placeholder (listed under Needs review: TalkBack reads the placeholder while the field is empty, but the field may have no name once something is typed) or an entered value -- which still doesn't prove the field has no name at all, since Android can also name a field through android:labelFor/getLabeledBy(), which the harness does not read yet, so that case is Needs review too. Without the harness at all, none of this is available.
- **Impact:** When the harness ran: a field with a real hint is not flagged; a field showing a placeholder that Android doesn't also expose as hint text is listed under Needs review (4.1.2); a field showing an entered value with no hint, description or (readable) label is also listed under Needs review (4.1.2), because it may still be labelled via android:labelFor. When the harness did not run, a text field whose only text is its visible text is listed under Needs review (4.1.2) for the same underlying reason, worded more generally.
- **Check manually:** For a field listed under Needs review, check with TalkBack that it is announced with a name (including one linked with android:labelFor), not just its content.

### Google's Accessibility Test Framework needs the instrumentation harness to install and run

`android-atf-harness` · Limitation · Detection · rules: `atf`

- **What:** A small test app runs Google's Accessibility Test Framework (ATF) 4.1.1 against the app under test through UiAutomation, without changing it, and also reads a few extra accessibility properties uiautomator dump does not (isShowingHintText, hint text, isHeading, paneTitle, stateDescription, isImportantForAccessibility). Swipewalk ships this harness prebuilt (installed with adb; no JDK, Gradle or network access needed) and installs it automatically on first use, replacing an older install left on the device by a previous Swipewalk version. Only a maintainer's own harness build (--android-harness, an option for working on Swipewalk) is built with Gradle instead, which needs a JDK and the Android SDK. If it can't be built (the --android-harness path only) or installed, or a run fails (a device policy, a flaky instrumentation run), the scan continues without it and says so.
- **Impact:** ATF's 14 checks (ClassName, ClickableSpan, DuplicateClickableBounds, DuplicateSpeakableText, EditableContentDesc, ImageContrast, LinkPurposeUnclear, RedundantDescription, SpeakableTextPresent, TextContrast, TextSize, TouchTargetSize, TraversalOrder, UnexposedText -- though UnexposedTextCheck needs text recognition the harness does not supply and never produces a finding, and TextSizeCheck reported on one device but not another scanning the same screen, for a reason not yet pinned down, see "partial-wcag-coverage") and the extra properties above are unavailable for that scan; the report and results.json say Google's checks did not run and why, and the WCAG coverage section shows the affected criteria as not tested rather than silently reporting nothing.
- **Check manually:** If Google's checks keep being skipped, the report and results.json give the reason for each screen; otherwise test by hand with TalkBack.

### Page-title check needs the harness, and can't tell "no title" from "can't read it" on Android 8.0/8.1

`android-page-title` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `page-titled`

- **What:** The page-titled check reads only AccessibilityNodeInfo#getPaneTitle() (API 28), which the instrumentation harness only reports when it actually ran for that capture (see "android-atf-harness"); when it didn't run, the check doesn't run either rather than assume there's no title. It does not read the separate window title (AccessibilityWindowInfo#getTitle(), API 24), which TalkBack also announces and which the check has no way to credit -- confirmed on BuggyApp's MainPage, which sets a MAUI Page.Title shown in its NavigationPage toolbar and has two on-screen headings, yet still has no pane title, so the check fires there. On Android 8.0/8.1 (API 26-27: at or above the harness's own minSdk 26, but below getPaneTitle's API 28), the harness runs but can never read a pane title on any screen, so the check reports "no pane title exposed" for every screen on those two OS versions regardless of whether one is actually set. Not implemented on iOS: XCUITest exposes a "navigationBar" element (used elsewhere only to crop screenshots), but nothing has verified that its presence or title reliably matches WCAG2ICT's "software titled" concept across screen types (tab-bar-only screens, sheets, screens without a navigation bar by design).
- **Impact:** No 2.4.2 check runs at all when the harness didn't run. A screen whose title is only a window title (not a pane title) is flagged even though a screen reader may announce that window title. On Android 8.0/8.1 specifically, every screen is flagged for review even when it has a title. No automated 2.4.2 check on iOS.
- **Check manually:** Check each screen has a title describing its purpose, announced by the screen reader on screen change, on every platform and OS version.

### android:labelFor / getLabeledBy() associations aren't read

`android-labelfor` · Limitation · Detection · rules: `missing-name`

- **What:** Android lets a visible label name a field it isn't the content of, via android:labelFor (XML) or View#setLabelFor()/getLabeledBy() -- TalkBack is documented to use this to announce the label together with the field. Confirmed 2026-09-23 with NativeAndroid's Views screen: a field labelled this way produces an uiautomator dump node identical to a genuinely unlabelled one (empty content-desc, empty hint); uiautomator dump's XML has no attribute for the relationship at all, and the instrumentation harness does not currently read getLabeledBy() either. Not tested with TalkBack directly.
- **Impact:** missing-name reports a field labelled only via android:labelFor exactly like an unlabelled one -- a false positive if TalkBack does announce the association as documented.
- **Check manually:** For a text field flagged by missing-name, check whether its visible label is wired up with android:labelFor before treating it as unlabelled; confirm with TalkBack that the label is (or isn't) announced.

### A name set inside a Jetpack Compose button can land on a different uiautomator node than its clickable one

`android-compose-merged-name` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `label-in-name`, `identifier-name`, `atf`, `screen-reader-label-in-name`

- **What:** Verified 2026-09-23 with NativeAndroid's Compose screen: for several IconButtons/Buttons whose accessible name is set with contentDescription on a child Icon() or with Modifier.semantics { contentDescription = ... } on the button itself, uiautomator dump's clickable="true", focusable="true" node reports an empty content-desc, and the name appears only on a separate, non-clickable child node (confirmed in the raw dump; bounds and the name are both present, just on a different node). One IconButton on the same screen, built the same way but with contentDescription = null, correctly showed up as an unlabeled clickable button, and a TextField's label = { ... } parameter correctly named the field -- so this isn't every Compose control, and the exact condition that causes the split hasn't been pinned down. Partly addressed 2026-09-23 for the unambiguous case: when exactly one non-focusable descendant carries a name and nothing else in the subtree is independently focusable or clickable, UiAutomatorParser.TryMergeDescendantName gives the clickable node that name as its own Label, approximating how a screen reader is expected to read the merged node together (matching the existing ScreenReaderPredictor.AccessibleName fallback, but now also seen by rules that read AccessibilityNode.Label directly). Extended 2026-09-26 for one several-named-descendants shape: exactly one descendant carrying only a content-desc, and exactly one other carrying only plain visible text, nothing else named in the subtree. The one real button confirmed with this shape is NativeAndroid's N5 -- Modifier.semantics { contentDescription = "Submit" } set directly on the Button itself (not on an icon; N5 has no icon), with a separate Text("Pay") child -- and real TalkBack captures of that exact button on both the Android emulator (TalkBack 16.0.0, 2026-09-23, re-confirmed in two separate device sessions on 2026-09-26) and a physical Pixel 4a (TalkBack 17.0.1, two separate device sessions on 2026-09-26) announce BOTH parts, in the same order (content-desc, then visible text, then role) every time -- "Submit || Pay || Button" on the emulator (three separate utterances, joined by Swipewalk's own harness) and "Submit. Pay. Button." on the Pixel (TalkBack 17 sent it as one combined utterance with sentence-final periods, which this comparator already parses the same way -- see ScreenReaderCaptureComparer.TryStripTrailingWord's ". " separator; see also docs/case-study.md "Real TalkBack capture, in five languages"). The parser now merges this tree shape wherever it occurs (the same shape can occur on classic Android Views, not only Compose, though only this one Compose button has real TalkBack evidence behind it): the clickable node's Label becomes the full joined name ("Submit, Pay") and its VisibleText becomes the text part ("Pay"), which is what lets label-in-name evaluate the node at all -- though by that same construction the merged name always contains the merged VisibleText, so label-in-name can never report a mismatch for this exact shape either way (see Impact). Still deliberately NOT merged: a several-named-descendants shape with more than one contentDescription candidate, more than one plain-text candidate, or a descendant that carries both its own content-desc and its own visible text -- which one (or in what order) would actually be announced isn't established for those shapes, so this still doesn't guess.
- **Impact:** identifier-name now reports the clickable element's real role (e.g. "button" instead of "group") for the single-named-descendant case. This role fix does NOT extend to the new N5 (one contentDescription + one text descendant) shape: the content-desc descendant's own Label is deliberately left in place there (not cleared), so that a developer-identifier name on it is still caught by identifier-name -- with the pre-existing wrong (non-clickable) role, same as before this change, rather than silenced entirely (clearing it would have erased the finding, since a name containing the required ", " join never looks like a developer identifier). Untested on a real screen either way, since neither N5's "Submit" nor "Pay" looks like a developer identifier. missing-name's own result is unchanged -- it already found these buttons named through ScreenReaderPredictor.AccessibleName's descendant-walk fallback, so the model-level fix only makes that more robust for other rules, not a behavior change for missing-name itself. Corrected assumption: target-size was never blocked by this gap -- it already reads the clickable node's own (correct) bounds regardless of naming; a measured 48x48dp Compose IconButton not tripping target-size is IconButton's own minimum-touch-target padding (similar to BuggyApp's B5, though B5 enlarges to only 44dp and still trips the platform advisory), not this naming gap. Changed for N5's exact shape: label-in-name now evaluates NativeAndroid's N5 button and reports no mismatch, consistent with real TalkBack capture on both the emulator and a physical Pixel 4a on 2026-09-26, in two separate device sessions (this change's own, and the TalkBack-completeness fix's below) -- confirmed live on both devices both times, not only from the saved fixture. That is TalkBack evidence, not proof of a WCAG 2.5.3 pass: whether Android Voice Access would actually activate N5's button by saying "Pay" hasn't been tested. This also means the tree alone can no longer show a real 2.5.3 mismatch for this specific shape (a content-desc descendant plus a separate text descendant, nothing else named): by construction the merged name always contains the merged visible text, so a genuine override that hides the visible text from screen readers -- the case label-in-name exists to catch -- would need a different shape (for example the button's own content-desc set directly, not merged from a child) to be caught. Still open: a several-named-descendants button with more than one contentDescription candidate, more than one text candidate, or a descendant carrying both its own content-desc and visible text, is still left entirely unlabeled (Label and VisibleText both null), and identifier-name still reports the wrong (non-clickable) role for those shapes, since nothing is merged there. Google's Accessibility Test Framework's ImageContrastCheck also reported nothing for a low-contrast icon built the same way, for a reason not determined. With --screen-reader, screen-reader-label-in-name (added 2026-09-25) adds independent, capture-based coverage on top of the tree-only merge for two of the several-named-descendants shapes: the one now merged (through the node's own VisibleText) and an unmerged shape with exactly one visible-text candidate (through ScreenReaderLabelInNameRule.SingleDescendantVisibleText) -- it compares a control's visible text against what TalkBack actually said, rather than assuming the tree's merged name is correct, so a genuine mismatch the parser's construction can't reveal would still surface there. It does NOT cover a shape with more than one visible-text candidate, which SingleDescendantVisibleText also declines as ambiguous. This check runs whenever a capture reaches every focusable or interactive element it found and TalkBack said something for each (see "android-screen-reader-capture") -- fixed 2026-09-26 (ruleset 2026.09.28): the Android helper previously reported every capture as incomplete regardless of outcome, so this check could never fire on real device data before that fix; the N5 captures above are the first to meet that condition, on both devices.
- **Check manually:** For a Compose or Views button whose visible text and accessible name might differ across separate descendants -- merged by the parser or not -- check with TalkBack what is actually announced, and with speech input (Voice Access) whether saying the visible text activates it; the tree-only checks can never show a mismatch for the one shape this parser merges, so this manual check matters most there.

### TalkBack capture is opt-in, checks only some of the screen, and silences the phone while it runs

`android-screen-reader-capture` · Limitation · ScreenReader · rules: `screen-reader-capture`, `screen-reader-label-in-name`

- **What:** With --screen-reader, the instrumentation harness turns TalkBack on, moves accessibility focus to each focusable/interactive element in Swipewalk's own tree order (not TalkBack's own swipe order -- this checks what TalkBack says about an element, not its navigation order), and reads back exactly what TalkBack said. This works by temporarily making a small app Swipewalk installs (labelled "Swipewalk (testing only)" in the device's text-to-speech settings) the device's default text-to-speech engine: Google's TalkBack sends its speech to whichever engine that setting names, seen with both TalkBack 16 and 17, so Swipewalk's engine receives the exact utterance text and reports it back, entirely on-device (an earlier design read TalkBack's on-screen caption with an OCR library; that approach and its one non-local-only exception are gone). Swipewalk's engine does not speak the text through anything else -- TalkBack is effectively silent for the length of the capture (a pass-through to the phone's normal engine was tried and removed: it made TalkBack repeat itself in a fast, unbounded loop). Don't run this on a phone someone is relying on TalkBack with right now. Because this changes accessibility settings, every SETTING it changes (which service is enabled, touch exploration, the default text-to-speech engine) is restored on three independent paths: the capture's own restore when it finishes normally; a marker file read back at the start of the next --screen-reader run or by pre-flight, if the process was killed before its own restore ran; and a timer armed on the device itself before anything changes, re-armed roughly every 20 seconds while the walk keeps making progress, and cancelled on a normal finish, which restores those settings on its own if Swipewalk stops responding or is disconnected from the phone -- verified on a Pixel 4a by killing both the host command and the on-device capture process and confirming the phone put the settings back with no computer involved, within about 90 seconds of the last time that timer was armed or re-armed, when an exact alarm is allowed on the device (a locked-down device without that permission falls back to an inexact alarm, which can be several minutes later); an absolute ceiling of about 10 minutes from the first arm applies no matter how many times it is re-armed after that, so a walk that never finishes still can't hold the safety net off indefinitely. The helper app itself is uninstalled once every changed setting reads back as restored, which removes its WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS grant with it; only a restore that failed or could not be confirmed leaves it installed (the on-device safety timer above and `doctor`'s own leftover-repair both live inside it, so removing it early would break exactly the safety net this is about). This does mean a `record` session with --screen-reader on for several screens reinstalls and grants the app again before each one. On a physical phone, --screen-reader asks for confirmation before any of this (a non-interactive run needs --screen-reader-confirm instead); use a test device regardless. The text-to-speech routing was verified on a Pixel 4a (Android 13, TalkBack 17.0.1) and the Android emulator (TalkBack 16.0.0); an older TalkBack version was seen to split one element's name and its role word into two separate utterances rather than one combined announcement, which the comparator now recovers correctly. The comparison across languages was verified on an Android emulator with the system language set to English, Spanish, Hindi, Arabic and Japanese: TalkBack said its own role and hint words in that language in every case, but did not translate the app's own accessible names in any of them, so a localized role word alone (for example Spanish "Botón") is not reported as a name difference -- the trade-off is that a genuine difference could go unreported when nothing was predicted for that element to begin with, EXCEPT when the text looks like a developer identifier rather than a plausible role word. That exception catches a real problem the tree alone can't show, seen on BuggyApp regardless of language: a button with an empty accessible name in the tree, which TalkBack nonetheless announced as "btnCancelPayment" (that button's AutomationId, planted as bug B7 -- where TalkBack itself got that text wasn't determined). Because that text looks like a developer identifier, it is still reported as a difference even on a device whose language this has no role vocabulary for. Plain text isn't captured (only focusable/interactive elements are, to keep the cost down, roughly 1-2 seconds per element); this capture counts as "complete" when every focusable/interactive element the walk found was reached and TalkBack said something for it, not when the whole screen (plain text included) was covered -- the report never describes this route as covering the whole screen. An element TalkBack said nothing for makes the whole screen's capture "not complete", with a reason naming how many (a silent element is never reported as a finding itself); if nothing comes back at all for the first couple of elements, the capture stops with a reason rather than walking the rest of the screen for nothing (a managed device or a phone maker's own TalkBack build may not honor the text-to-speech engine setting). The same thing happens if TalkBack goes quiet for several elements in a row after having said something for at least one earlier element on the same screen -- the capture stops there too, with its own reason, rather than spending the full per-element wait on every remaining element only to report each one as silent. The desktop app's screen reader session uses a different pass-through mode that is switched off for this capture; see "android-live-screen-reader-session".
- **Impact:** Off by default: without --screen-reader, screen-reader evidence stays predicted only (see "predicted-screen-reader"), and nothing on the device changes. With it: TalkBack speaks nothing aloud for the length of the capture; a screen with many elements takes noticeably longer to scan; plain text and silently-skipped elements are never checked at all; a managed device, a locked-down TTS setting, or a TalkBack build this hasn't been verified against skips the whole capture for a screen, with a reason shown in the report, rather than reporting something unreliable; and a `record` session that checks several screens reinstalls and re-grants the helper app before each one, since it's removed again as soon as each capture's restore succeeds.
- **Check manually:** Swipe through plain text by hand (it isn't captured), and compare the report's captured transcript against a manual TalkBack pass if a finding looks surprising.

### The Android (TalkBack) live screen-reader session checks the first screen most fully, and is unverified in a few ways

`android-live-screen-reader-session` · Limitation · ScreenReader

- **What:** The live screen-reader session (desktop app: Screen reader session page; CLI: `swipewalk session`) lets a tester use TalkBack on the phone exactly as they normally would while Swipewalk passively records what happens, instead of Swipewalk driving TalkBack itself for a bounded, silent walk the way --screen-reader does. It uses a DIFFERENT pass-through mode from --screen-reader's own (see "android-screen-reader-capture"): the helper app also forwards each utterance to Google's speech engine (`com.google.android.tts`, hard-bound -- not necessarily the phone's own configured engine, so the voice may differ) so the tester can hear TalkBack while Swipewalk keeps recording the exact text. This pass-through mode is switched OFF at the start of every --screen-reader capture and by the on-device safety timer's own restore, so a killed session can't make a later silent capture speak. Captured text proves the exact words TalkBack produced. The pass-through speech was heard once, by a person, on one physical Pixel phone, after raising the phone's media volume: during a session Swipewalk plays TalkBack's speech through the phone's media volume, so a low media volume means silence, while Swipewalk records the words either way. The start-of-session "Can you hear TalkBack?" sound check was heard the same way, on that one phone. Only the session's FIRST screen (the one already open when the session starts) gets a real capture and screenshot to compare against for 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value and 1.1.1 Non-text Content evidence -- a normal capture cannot run while the session's own instrumentation holds the device's one UiAutomation connection, so a screen reached later in the session has no capture to build one from. Every screen the session visited is shown in the report the same way as a scanned screen; a screen reached later says plainly that Swipewalk's automated checks and predicted transcript did not run on it. Its picture is separate from that capture: every newly seen screen state (up to three per screen) gets a plain screenshot, taken shortly after the screen is detected (a plain screenshot does not need that connection), with a numbered outline on each control TalkBack reached and a dashed outline on each control it did not. A state gets no picture if the tester had already moved on, had left the app, or the screenshot failed, and outlines are placed from each control's recorded position, so they can be off if the screen changed between detection and the screenshot; the report's text lists carry the same information. The time each screenshot adds has not been measured on a device. A session's run is saved while it runs (at once for each new screen, screen state or note, otherwise about every 2 seconds while what TalkBack reached changes), so one whose Swipewalk process is killed or crashes is listed as ended early with everything up to its last save, and the last few seconds before it stopped may be missing; the phone's accessibility settings may then still need putting back with Check or `swipewalk doctor`. A saved session can be continued later (`swipewalk session --continue`, or Continue session in History): new screens are added, and a screen opened again replaces its earlier recording in that run, so the report shows only the newer recording of it, while the run's saved event log keeps the earlier events. That later screen's controls are still identified by an exact-match id only (the harness computes a node identity live, from the same tree walk it already does to track focus, mirroring the identity scheme a normal capture would compute but not verified byte-for-byte against one), which is enough for 2.5.3 Label in Name evidence (comparing what TalkBack said against the control's own visible text) to fire on any screen, not only the first. A screen's own identity is a fingerprint of its focusable/interactive controls' roles and names (excluding a text field's typed value, so typing doesn't look like a new screen); two screens with no focusable/interactive controls at all (for example two different plain loading screens) are indistinguishable by this and would count as the same screen. A control's identity also includes its on-screen position, so scrolling a list can make an already-reached control look like a new, not-yet-reached one at its new position -- reported as a coverage gap, not a finding, but still worth knowing. Seen on an Android emulator (2026-09-28, BuggyApp and NativeAndroid): while a screen's layout is still settling in the first moment after it appears (inset or scroll-position adjustments), the same control can be recorded at two different positions. The identity used for node matching and the one the control is later reached and spoken at can then become two separate entries -- a control reached this way can show up as not reached (a coverage gap) and may get no 2.5.3 evidence at all. In that test, 2.5.3 evidence still appeared on a later screen, for a control whose position had already settled by the time the tester reached it. Reduced 2026-09-28: the harness now re-reads a screen's controls (comparing the same node-identity set used for matching) until two consecutive reads agree, for up to about 1.5 seconds, instead of trusting the first read. This targets both the split identities described above and controls missing from a first read taken too early. In one test on the Android emulator (BuggyApp's first screen) the live session then found 11 controls, the same number a normal scan's uiautomator dump found for that screen; before this change it found fewer. NativeAndroid was not re-tested. A screen that takes longer than about 1.5 seconds to settle, or one that never stops changing (a live-updating banner, a spinner), can still show these gaps -- the harness uses its last read rather than waiting indefinitely. No gesture classification yet: every focus move is reported as a generic move, so no 2.4.3 Focus Order/1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence evidence is ever shown -- the report says plainly that this evidence isn't available, never a stronger claim. Android only: the iPhone (VoiceOver) session (desktop app, or `swipewalk session --platform ios`) is a different, per-screen design (see "ios-voiceover-captions-capture").
- **Impact:** Android only (`swipewalk session --platform android` and the desktop app's Android option); the iPhone (VoiceOver) option is described in "ios-voiceover-captions-capture". Real evidence for the first screen (4.1.2/1.1.1/2.5.3); for a later screen, only 2.5.3 evidence, with no normal capture or predicted-transcript comparison (a plain screenshot with reached and not-reached outlines may still be shown). Two content-free screens (or a scrolled list) can be misread as the same/different screen than they really are, as described above. A control reached while its screen was still settling may be counted twice (once matched, once reached) and miss its 2.5.3 evidence entirely. No focus-order evidence is ever shown. The speech and the sound check have been heard on only one phone, after raising its media volume; a low media volume means the tester hears nothing, though the recording is unaffected.
- **Check manually:** For a screen reached after the first, compare the report's live-session evidence against a manual TalkBack pass if a finding looks surprising; for focus order, judge it by ear during the session itself, since Swipewalk doesn't show it in the report yet.
- **Planned:** Trying the pass-through and the sound check on more phones; gesture classification on real hardware so focus-order evidence can be shown; a real capture (and 4.1.2/1.1.1 evidence) for screens after the first; focus-following on iOS/VoiceOver (the iPhone option reads captions per screen only).

### Custom accessibility action labels are shown, but not checked

`android-custom-action-labels` · Limitation · ScreenReader

- **What:** When the instrumentation harness ran (see "android-atf-harness"), it also reads each node's action list (AccessibilityNodeInfo#getActionList(), API 21) and reports every non-blank action label -- uiautomator dump has no field for a node's action list at all, so this is otherwise invisible to Swipewalk. It covers two things it cannot tell apart: a genuinely separate custom action (Jetpack Compose's customActions property, e.g. CustomAccessibilityAction(label = "Remove article from list") -- documented to appear in TalkBack's own actions menu) and a label placed on a standard action such as click (Compose's Modifier.semantics { onClick(label = ...) }, confirmed used in Google's own Now in Android sample app to rename what an accessibility service announces as the action -- not documented the same way). Any labels found are shown in the predicted transcript as a note to check on the device (Android's Jetpack Compose accessibility guide, for the custom-action case only: "An accessibility service like TalkBack then highlights the component, and hints that there are more actions available in its menu" -- developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics, checked 2026-09-27), never folded into the predicted spoken text as if it were confirmed wording.
- **Impact:** No rule evaluates these labels yet. Whether a custom action can have a blank label at all, and what TalkBack does with one if it can, has not been checked. Real device verification is pending: this was checked by parsing (unit tests only), not against a real captured tree from a device or emulator.
- **Check manually:** For a screen whose predicted transcript shows a note about action labels, open TalkBack's actions menu (or Voice Access) for that element and check every action has a clear name.
- **Planned:** A rule for a genuinely custom action with no label, once the harness also captures each action's id so it can be told apart from a standard action that simply has no label (the normal case for most controls), and once a blank-label custom action and TalkBack's own handling of it have been confirmed on a device.

### WebView content needs TalkBack registered, done automatically only on an emulator

`android-webview-accessibility-physical` · Limitation · Detection

- **What:** A WebView's DOM only mirrors into Android's accessibility tree once a real, registered AccessibilityService is bound to the device (confirmed 2026-09-28: setting accessibility_enabled directly, and the instrumentation harness's own UiAutomation connection, are both NOT enough on their own -- only a real service such as TalkBack triggers it, with no app restart needed). On an emulator, Swipewalk detects an empty WebView node in the first dump and briefly registers TalkBack itself to re-read it, restoring the setting immediately after (the same mechanism --screen-reader already uses, narrowed to just this one setting). On a physical device this is NOT done automatically: registering an accessibility service on someone's real phone without being asked is exactly the risk --screen-reader's own physical-device confirmation prompt exists for, and this WebView check runs on every plain scan/record, with no matching prompt of its own -- so it stays emulator-only rather than adding a second, differently-shaped confirmation flow for the same risk. --screen-reader does not currently help here either: it registers TalkBack only for its own, separate transcript-capture step, which runs after the tree Swipewalk's rules read has already been captured, so a physical-device scan still sees the WebView as empty even with --screen-reader on.
- **Impact:** On a physical Android device, a screen whose WebView content has not already been made visible some other way (for example TalkBack already running for real) is scanned as if the WebView were empty: every rule (missing-name, target-size, text-contrast and the rest) sees no content inside it at all.
- **Check manually:** On a physical Android device, test a WebView's content by hand with TalkBack; it isn't in the scanned tree.
- **Planned:** Making a physical-device scan see WebView content too, most likely by having the --screen-reader confirmation also cover this narrower setting change, once verified on real hardware.

### The axe-core web-content audit (--web-audit) needs a debug build, and can't always place a finding on the report's screenshot

`android-webview-axe-audit` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `axe`

- **What:** scan --web-audit runs axe-core (Deque's engine, bundled unmodified) directly inside a WebView's own page, over the Chrome DevTools Protocol: it needs the app under test to be a debug build (or otherwise built with WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true), which a Debug build enables with no extra code -- confirmed 2026-09-28), and a WebView actually open on screen; otherwise it's skipped with a reason. Because axe-core runs entirely inside the WebView's own DOM, it knows nothing about Swipewalk's accessibility tree -- AxeNodeMatcher matches its flagged element back to a specific tree node conservatively, by the element's DOM id (which reaches Android's resource-id, confirmed by testing), its aria-label/alt, or its own inner text, only when exactly one node matches; an ambiguous or unmatched element is reported at the screen level instead, with the flagged HTML in the message, rather than guessed. A general CSS-selector-to-node matcher (needed once a real page has more than a handful of similar elements) is not built. Only axe-core's own WCAG A/AA rules are run (its best-practice, experimental and WCAG-AAA-only rules are excluded -- see docs/checks.md's "Runs under --web-audit" column, which also lists five rules that carry a real WCAG tag but never run because axe-core also marks them experimental). If a process has more than one WebView open, the audit picks the first page target the WebView's devtools endpoint lists, which may not be the one on screen. axe-core audits the whole loaded DOM of the top-level page, including content scrolled out of view; content inside an iframe in the WebView (same-origin or cross-origin) is not audited, because Swipewalk injects axe-core only into the top-level page.
- **Impact:** On a screen with several visually or textually similar elements, some axe-core findings may not be placed on the report's screenshot or matched to a specific line in the accessibility tree, only named by their flagged HTML. --web-audit does nothing at all on a release/store build, unless the app itself calls WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true). When this screen's own captured tree has no WebView node at all, no axe-core finding is reported and the check does not count as run for this screen, even when a WebView elsewhere in the app's process still answers over its own devtools socket from an earlier or different screen -- that audit still happens (nothing here stops the underlying CDP call), its result is simply discarded rather than attributed to a screen it has nothing to do with. When the app's process has more than one WebView open (on this screen, or left over from another), findings may come from the wrong page or be shown under the wrong screenshot. Content inside an iframe in the WebView is not audited at all.
- **Check manually:** For a finding reported at the screen level ("could not be matched to a specific place"), find the flagged HTML in the WebView's own source. Build a debug configuration to use --web-audit at all.
- **Planned:** A general selector-to-node matcher, if a real page's density of similar elements makes the conservative matcher above too often ambiguous.

## Android, iOS · All frameworks

### Lost-content detection is a per-screen signal, not per-element

`large-text-lost-content-heuristic` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `large-text-lost-content`

- **What:** large-text-lost-content compares the normal and large-text accessibility trees for a screen and flags controls or text present at normal size that are gone at the larger size. It reports them only when the large-text tree has no scrollable container anywhere on the screen: on Android, uiautomator dump omits nodes that are entirely off-screen -- whole containers, not just their leaves (verified 2026-09-23 on a Pixel 4a: an off-screen HorizontalStackLayout was missing along with its children) -- so the rule can't reliably trace which container a specific missing element belonged to. If the screen has any scrollable region at all, missing elements are assumed reachable by scrolling there, even if they actually sat in a different, non-scrolling part of the screen. On iOS this check has not been verified on a device: XCUITest's snapshot usually still includes elements positioned past the screen edge (unlike uiautomator dump), so content pushed off-screen there may not show up as missing at all, and IsScrollable means "is a scroll/table/collection view" rather than "has something to scroll right now", which is a different signal than the Android one this was verified against.
- **Impact:** A genuine loss of content or functionality can go unreported on a screen that also has an unrelated scrollable region. It can also flag text that simply changed between the two captures (a timer, a clock, a live count, a carousel, a toast or snackbar shown in only one of the two), or an element that was renamed rather than removed.
- **Check manually:** On a screen with a scrollable region, also check by hand at 200% text size (Android) or your platform's largest text size whether every control present at normal size can still be reached, especially outside that scrollable area.

## iOS · All frameworks

### On a physical iPhone the large-text check drives the Settings app

`ios-large-text-physical-settings` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** On a physical iPhone, scan --large-text and record set Larger Text to AX3 (about 235%) through the Settings app, return to the app, and restore the original setting afterwards. This takes a couple of minutes per screen and needs the phone unlocked.
