The Settings layout can change between iOS versions; if the path isn't found, Swipewalk uses a per-app text-size launch setting instead, and otherwise skips the check with a reason.
- **Impact:** On a new iOS version the check may fall back or be skipped until Swipewalk is updated; the report says which method was used or why the check was skipped.
- **Check manually:** If the check was skipped, set Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Larger Text to a large size and check each screen by hand.

### The appearance rescan is skipped on a physical iPhone left on Automatic

`appearance-physical-iphone-automatic` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** scan --appearance both works on a physical iPhone by driving Settings > Appearance (reading the current choice, switching to the other explicit appearance, then restoring it), the same as the iOS Simulator (`simctl ui appearance`) and Android (`cmd uimode night`). A device set to Automatic (day/night scheduling) has no single "current" appearance to switch from, so that case is left untouched and the check is skipped with a reason rather than guessed. Verified on iOS 27 (where the Light/Dark picker lives on its own "Appearance" screen, separate from Display & Brightness); on another iOS version the Settings layout may differ, and the check is skipped there with a reason too rather than driving the wrong screen.
- **Impact:** On a physical iPhone set to Automatic, only whichever appearance the device happened to be showing is checked; a contrast failure that only shows up in the other appearance is missed unless the phone is set to Light or Dark by hand and scanned again in each.
- **Check manually:** On a physical iPhone, set Settings > Appearance to Light or Dark (instead of Automatic) and scan again in each.

### The orientation rescan can't read a physical iPhone's rotation lock state

`orientation-physical-iphone-rotation-lock` · Limitation · Coverage

- **What:** scan --orientation both rotates a physical iPhone the same way as the iOS Simulator, through the scanning harness's XCUIDevice.shared.orientation (there is no `simctl` equivalent). On a physical device this is a simulated sensor event, and there is no public API to read Control Center's rotation lock state, so Swipewalk shows a heads-up before rotating a physical iPhone but cannot tell whether the lock was on. In a real test (iOS 27.0, iPhone SE, rotation lock deliberately left on), the interface still rotated -- so at least on that iOS version, the simulated event was not simply swallowed by the lock. That single observation doesn't rule out a different result on another iOS version, so a screen that looks the same after rotating is still reported for review the same way a genuinely orientation-restricted screen is (never as a confirmed WCAG failure either way).
- **Impact:** On an iOS version where rotation lock does block the simulated rotation (not seen in one test on iOS 27.0, iPhone SE, but not ruled out on other versions or devices), a physical iPhone with the lock on could report a screen as restricted to one orientation when it actually supports both.
- **Check manually:** If --orientation both flags a screen on a physical iPhone, turn Control Center's rotation lock off and rotate the device by hand to confirm whether it's a real restriction -- rotating with the lock on won't move the app either way. Turning the lock off before scanning also removes this particular doubt, though one test on iOS 27.0 found the interface rotated even with the lock on.

### iOS overlays over the app may be captured while recording

`ios-overlays-during-recording` · Limitation · Detection

- **What:** Record mode captures only while the app under test is in front, but iOS can report the app as in front while Notification Center or Control Center is pulled down over it.
- **Impact:** A screenshot taken at that moment could include notifications.
- **Check manually:** Don't open Notification Center or Control Center while recording, and review screenshots before sharing reports.

### A device .ipa must be signed for that device to be installed

`ios-install-unsigned-ipa` · Limitation · Devices

- **What:** Any installed app can be scanned, whoever signed it. But iOS only installs an .ipa file signed for the device: a development or ad-hoc build whose profile includes it, or an enterprise build. App Store .ipa files cannot be sideloaded, and Swipewalk does not re-sign apps.
- **Impact:** Builds signed for other devices, or App Store builds from a file, cannot be installed and scanned from the file.
- **Check manually:** Install the app through TestFlight, the App Store or your MDM and scan it by --bundle-id, or scan a Simulator build.
- **Planned:** Installing builds signed for other devices

### Physical iPhones: slower recording, some checks unverified

`ios-physical-devices` · Limitation · Devices

- **What:** scan and record work on physical iPhones and iPads (tested on an iPhone with iOS 18.6). The harness is signed with a fitting installed development profile (no Apple ID needed) or Xcode automatic signing, and exchanges files through devicectl. Each check of the screen takes several seconds, so new screens are noticed with a delay. The first run asks for Face ID or the passcode to allow UI automation. Manual signing with a hand-installed profile, and the pause when another app comes to the front during recording, are covered by tests but not yet confirmed on hardware. Bringing the app to the front (or starting it) when a scan or recording begins was verified on the Simulator only.
- **Impact:** Recording on a physical device notices screen changes a few seconds late. If the in-front check does not work on a device, other apps are still not captured unless a new screen of the target app appears while they are in front.
- **Check manually:** Wait for each screen to be reported before moving on, don't switch apps while recording, and review screenshots before sharing reports.

### XCUITest doesn't expose isAccessibilityElement or traits

`ios-accessibility-element` · Limitation · Detection

- **What:** Whether VoiceOver can reach an element is approximated from its type and label. Traits such as header and adjustable are not visible to the scanner through XCUITest. With --screen-reader's Accessibility Inspector route (see "ios-inspector-walk-capture"), traits ARE visible for the elements it walks -- but only for a small, deliberately conservative subset of predicted roles (button, link, image, heading, slider) that this is confident the Inspector's trait vocabulary can confirm or deny; a role Swipewalk never predicted in the first place (for example a heading with no visible sign of being one) is still not found even then.
- **Impact:** Reachability can be predicted wrongly for custom views, so missing heading and control roles (1.3.1, 4.1.2) are not detected except where Apple's audit reports them, or where the Inspector route flags one of the small set of roles above as unconfirmed for review. On a screen with an Accessibility Inspector capture, the "Screen reader (captured)" tab's "Evidence for WCAG coverage" section lists the elements the Inspector reported with the Header trait, for 1.3.1 -- this is evidence for the manual check (VoiceOver itself is not turned on for it, and it cannot show text that looks like a heading but isn't exposed as one), never an automated finding or a status change.
- **Check manually:** Swipe through with VoiceOver and listen for the element type and state of each control.

### VoiceOver order is predicted from positions

`ios-geometric-order` · Limitation · ScreenReader

- **What:** The predicted swipe order sorts elements top to bottom and left to right. Custom accessibilityElements ordering set by the app is not visible. --screen-reader's Accessibility Inspector route captures the Inspector's own navigation order (Apple's tool for previewing what VoiceOver would read, not VoiceOver itself running) -- but an order difference from it isn't reported, on any screen: confirmed on a real device (2026-09-25) that the walk starts wherever the person clicked to set it up, not the top of the screen, and its order is circular, so an unanchored walk would look rotated relative to the predicted order in a way this can't tell apart from a genuine difference (see "ios-inspector-walk-capture").
- **Impact:** The predicted order may differ from VoiceOver's where the app customizes it; the Inspector route doesn't yet confirm or deny this either way.
- **Check manually:** Swipe through with VoiceOver and check the order is logical.

### The Accessibility Inspector route is opt-in and needs a person present

`ios-inspector-walk-capture` · Limitation · ScreenReader · rules: `screen-reader-capture`

- **What:** With --screen-reader on iOS, `scan` and `record` walk Xcode's Accessibility Inspector's Inspection menu ("Move to Next/Previous Item") over the macOS Accessibility API, reading its panel's label, value, traits, identifier, hint and class for each element the Inspector reaches. VoiceOver itself is never turned on -- this reports the Inspector's own view of the same accessibility properties VoiceOver would read, not real recorded speech. It needs the macOS Accessibility permission (System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility) for whichever app is responsible for the process running Swipewalk -- which lets that app operate other apps on the Mac, not only the Inspector, though Swipewalk itself only ever uses it for the Inspector -- asked for before the Inspector is used; if it's missing or declined, the run falls back to the predicted-only report with a clear reason recorded, never silently. It also needs a one-time manual step, per Inspector session, that has no Accessibility-API surface at all: opening Accessibility Inspector, choosing the target device in its own toolbar, and clicking the first element on the app's screen so the walk starts from the top -- both asked for directly by the prompt; if that click lands on the app's window or background rather than a real element, the walk is detected as implausible (every item empty, or far fewer items than the screen's predicted stops) and marked incomplete with a reason to click an element and scan again, rather than being reported as a clean, complete walk of nothing (found on a real device, 2026-09-25, NativeiOS). "Per Inspector session" was observed to hold across one screen change, on a physical iPhone (2026-09-25, NativeiOS): after the one setup click, the person opened a different screen in the app with no more clicking in the Inspector at all, and the next scan's walk followed onto that new screen and captured it completely (17 elements) -- one data point, not a guarantee for every app or every screen change; if a walk comes back empty or short after navigating, click an element in the Inspector and scan again. In `record`, this one-time step is asked at most once per recording SESSION, not once per screen (a continued recording -- `record --continue` -- asks again, since resuming starts a new session with its own cache): the "Set up Accessibility Inspector" alert says so up front, and later screens in the same session reuse the answer silently; a screen whose own walk comes back short or incomplete is reported for that screen, with a prompt to click an element in the Inspector and press Scan this screen now again (the non-interactive path was verified on the iOS Simulator, 2026-09-26: a redirected `record --screen-reader --auto` run fell back to the predicted transcript at Screen 1 and never asked again -- recorded then as a decline; the current code records it as "not asked", since nobody was asked; an accepted walk reused across several recorded screens is not yet verified on a device). Because the Inspector reports no frame/geometry field, a captured element is matched to the scanned tree by its accessibility identifier first, then by its accessible name (disambiguating same-named elements by their native class where possible), then by position alone as a last resort -- recorded per item in results.json as Exact, Likely, Weak or unmatched, so a Weak or unmatched item is a hint to check by hand, not confirmed evidence of anything. The Inspector's own placeholder text for an unset field ("None", or "Empty string" for an empty text value) is normalized to nothing before matching or comparing, so it is never mistaken for a real name (found on a real device, 2026-09-25, BuggyApp) -- this does mean a genuine label or value that happens to be exactly that text is also treated as unset. A UIToolbar's own container and a scroll view's built-in scroll-position indicator each get a real XCUITest accessibility label ("Toolbar", "Vertical scroll bar, 1 page") -- on the same physical-iPhone capture, the Accessibility Inspector's own Next/Previous Item walk never stopped on either one (VoiceOver itself was not run, and it may still reach a scroll bar's indicator by touch even though this walk did not), so both are excluded from the predicted transcript entirely (a fix in the tree parser, not just this comparison), not only from this route's findings. Order differences from this route are not reported at all (see "ios-geometric-order"): confirmed on a real device that the walk starts wherever the person clicked, not the top of the screen, and the Inspector's navigation order is circular, so an unanchored walk looks rotated relative to the predicted order in a way this can't tell apart from a genuine difference.
- **Impact:** Off by default in both the CLI and the desktop app: it needs a person present every time it's used (the macOS Accessibility permission, then choosing the device and clicking an element in the Inspector -- once per recording session, not per screen), so it can't run unattended (a non-interactive run, or a declined/missing permission, falls back to the predicted-only report). Clicking the wrong thing (the app's window instead of an element) is caught and reported as incomplete rather than a false clean pass. A Weak-confidence or unmatched item is a hint to check by hand, not a confirmed name or role difference; only Exact and Likely matches are used for name and role comparisons. No order (1.3.2, 2.4.3) differences are reported from this route at all. A real label or value of exactly "None" or "Empty string" would be read as unset.
- **Check manually:** Swipe through with VoiceOver directly for anything the Inspector route was declined for, only partly captured, or matched with Weak confidence -- and for swipe order generally, since this route doesn't check it at all.
- **Planned:** A way to anchor the walk's starting point so order differences can be reported.

### VoiceOver-captions capture (--voiceover-captions) has been tried on only one real screen, in English

`ios-voiceover-captions-capture` · Limitation · ScreenReader · rules: `screen-reader-capture`

- **What:** With --voiceover-captions on `record`, or with `swipewalk session --platform ios` or the iPhone (VoiceOver) option on the desktop app's Screen reader session page, a person turns VoiceOver and its Caption Panel (Settings > Accessibility > VoiceOver > Caption Panel) on themselves and swipes through the screen, while this Mac polls the phone's screen over the cable (`xcrun devicectl device capture screenshot`, no XCUITest, no extra permission) and reads the on-screen caption text with Vision's on-device text recognition . VoiceOver is never scripted or turned on by Swipewalk. Consecutive identical captions are treated as one utterance; a caption disappearing and reappearing (the person swiped back to something they already heard) is treated as a new one. Each utterance is matched to a scanned tree node by a best-effort detection of VoiceOver's own on-screen cursor rectangle (overlap with the node's bounds), then by the caption text containing exactly one candidate's predicted accessible name -- checked against synthetic fixtures (drawn caption bars and cursor strokes on a plain background); reading a real Caption Panel was tried once on a real device (2026-09-28, physical iPhone SE, BuggyApp's first screen, English), but the cursor-rectangle detection itself is still unconfirmed against a real VoiceOver cursor. The capture is never reported complete: unlike a scripted walk, nothing here can tell whether the person swiped through the whole screen or stopped partway, so a predicted stop this didn't capture is never reported as Missing (see ScreenReaderCaptureRule). Unlike TalkBack's and the Accessibility Inspector's captures, an order difference from this source IS reported (1.3.2, 2.4.3): a person's real swipe order should be the reader's genuine navigation order, but the finding's own wording says this depends on the person swiping through the screen in one pass, start to finish -- swiping back and forth, or starting somewhere other than the first element, can make the order look different from the app's real order without that being a real problem. Whether the one real-device session above was swiped in one pass wasn't recorded, so order reporting from this route hasn't actually been confirmed on any screen, app or swipe style yet. Also untried beyond that one screen: the caption panel's timing (how long after an announcement the caption updates, and for how long it stays), OCR accuracy on a real Caption Panel's font/rendering on a busier screen or with more elements, and how a screen's other dark UI (a tab bar, a status/home indicator) affects the caption-region finder -- one real-device screenshot check (2026-09-26, no VoiceOver session, just proving the screenshot mechanism) found the iPhone's home-indicator bar can be mistaken for the caption region by the region-finder, though it produced no caption text there (Vision found nothing to read) so no false utterance resulted; a busier real caption session could differ. Tried in English only: other languages haven't been tried on a real device, and Vision's on-device text recognition supports only a fixed set of languages, queried at runtime via its own `VNRecognizeTextRequest.supportedRecognitionLanguages()` API, not necessarily every language a Caption Panel could show -- accuracy in any language besides English is unchecked on a real device. The desktop app's session page around this capture (choosing an iPhone, the ask-then-read-then-turn-VoiceOver-off steps, notes, Stop, saving the run as a "session") drives the same capture one screen at a time and was tried on a real iPhone SE with BuggyApp, in English: an earlier run showed two problems (reading ended by itself after 90 seconds before the finish button was pressed, and the on-page counts lagging one step) that were then fixed, and a later run (2026-09-29) worked as described at every step -- choosing the app, captions read, the finish step, the counts and the report showing the captions -- on that one device, with that one app, in English; it does not follow VoiceOver's focus between screens or list controls not reached, and it has no Next/Previous/Activate buttons. `swipewalk session --platform ios` runs the same engine code with typed commands but has not been run on a device yet.
- **Impact:** Off by default, on the command line `record` and `session --platform ios` only (in the desktop app, only through the iPhone option of the Screen reader session page), and tried against a real VoiceOver session on only one screen, in English -- treat evidence from this route as a first look to confirm by eye beyond that single tried case. A missed or wrongly-matched utterance is possible; the focus-rect detection especially is a coarse heuristic, still unconfirmed against a real VoiceOver cursor. An order-difference finding from this route assumes the person swiped through the screen in one pass, start to finish.
- **Check manually:** Swipe through with VoiceOver directly and compare by ear against the predicted transcript and whatever this route reported.
- **Planned:** Trying more screens, apps and eventually other languages on real devices; tightening the caption-region and focus-rect detectors against more real Caption Panel screenshots; deciding whether the poll interval needs adjusting once more real caption timing is known.

### Apple audit results are listed for review

`ios-apple-audit` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `engine`

- **What:** Issues from Apple's accessibility audit are included, but Apple does not document its thresholds against WCAG, so audit-only issues are marked Needs review.
- **Impact:** Some audit items may not be WCAG issues; some WCAG issues are outside the audit's scope.
- **Check manually:** Confirm each Apple audit item by hand before reporting it as a WCAG issue.

### A UIButton or SwiftUI Button built from a common SF Symbol may already have a name

`ios-sf-symbol-default-label` · Framework note · Rules · rules: `missing-name`

- **What:** Verified 2026-09-23 with NativeiOS: a UIButton/SwiftUI Button whose only content is UIImage(systemName: "magnifyingglass") (no accessibilityLabel set anywhere) was captured with the accessible name "Search" on both the Simulator and a physical iPhone. Apple appears to supply default accessibility descriptions for at least some SF Symbols, and UIKit/SwiftUI expose that description as the control's name when nothing else is set -- observed here for magnifyingglass only, not surveyed across other symbols. Android's equivalent (an ImageButton or Compose Icon with no contentDescription) has no such default -- confirmed on the same sample's Android screens, where the identical mistake correctly produces a missing-name finding.
- **Impact:** An icon-only button with no explicit accessible name produces no missing-name finding when its SF Symbol supplies a default one. That default describes the symbol (for example "Search" for a magnifying glass), not necessarily what the control does here -- a magnifying-glass icon used to zoom rather than search would get the same default name, and Swipewalk has no way to tell it's wrong for the context.
- **Check manually:** For an icon-only control, check with VoiceOver that the announced name actually describes what the control does here, not just that a name exists.

### SwiftUI's .accessibilityLabel() replaces a button's visible text in the captured tree

`ios-swiftui-accessibility-label-hides-text` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `label-in-name`

- **What:** Verified 2026-09-23 with NativeiOS: a SwiftUI Button("Pay") { }.accessibilityLabel("Submit") is captured with accessible name "Submit" and no trace of the visible text "Pay" anywhere in the tree. The equivalent UIKit button (a title "Pay" plus accessibilityLabel = "Submit") keeps "Pay" as a separate child node alongside the button's own "Submit" label, which is what label-in-name compares against.
- **Impact:** label-in-name cannot detect a label-in-name mismatch (WCAG 2.5.3) on a SwiftUI control whose visible text and accessible name were set this way: there is nothing left in the tree to compare the accessible name to, so the rule reports nothing, even though a sighted speech-input user sees one word and a screen reader announces another.
- **Check manually:** For a SwiftUI button, compare its visible text against what VoiceOver announces directly, rather than relying on label-in-name to catch a mismatch.

### The axe-core web-content audit (--web-audit) is Android only; not available on iOS yet

`ios-webview-axe-blocked` · Limitation · Rules · rules: `axe`

- **What:** WKWebView content has been seen in the XCUITest tree Swipewalk reads on iOS (a real app's map screen), so the ordinary rules should see it with no separate step (see the "Web content in apps (WebViews)" item in section 4 of the user guide); this was not checked against a WebView test page on iOS. The deeper axe-core audit (--web-audit) is not available on iOS: it would need a live Chrome-DevTools-Protocol-shaped connection into the WebView's own page, which on iOS means WKWebView.isInspectable (off by default for apps built with the iOS 16.4 SDK or later, including debug builds; on a physical device the Settings > Safari > Advanced > Web Inspector switch must also be on, while the Simulator always has it on). Checked on the iOS Simulator (2026-09-27): with isInspectable set in code, the bridge tool tried still found no debuggable target; the cause was not established. A physical iPhone was not tried.
- **Impact:** --web-audit does nothing on iOS; the coverage table lists the axe check as Android-only.
- **Check manually:** Test a WebView's own web content on iOS by connecting a Mac to the device/Simulator, opening it in Safari's own Web Inspector (Safari > Develop menu; an app built with the iOS 16.4 SDK or later must set isInspectable), then pasting axe-core's script into its console and running axe.run() by hand, separately from Swipewalk.
- **Planned:** Finding out why the Simulator exposed no inspectable target (for example trying a different bridge to Safari's Web Inspector protocol), or trying a physical iPhone, if real demand justifies the work.

## Windows · All frameworks

### Windows apps can't be scanned yet

`windows-not-supported` · Limitation · Devices

- **What:** The Windows collector (UI Automation with axe-windows) is not implemented.
- **Impact:** No automated results for Windows.
- **Check manually:** Test with Narrator and keyboard only, or use Accessibility Insights for Windows.
- **Planned:** Windows support

## Android · .NET MAUI

### MAUI tap gestures on labels are invisible on Android

`maui-android-tap-gesture` · Limitation · Detection

- **What:** A MAUI Label (or other view) with a TapGestureRecognizer is not marked clickable in Android's accessibility tree, so the scanner doesn't see it as a control.
- **Impact:** Target size and naming checks are skipped for such elements. Their button role is not exposed (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value), and TalkBack users may not be able to activate them.
- **Check manually:** With TalkBack on, double-tap every tappable text or image and check it works. Prefer Button or ImageButton; SemanticProperties.Description adds a name but not a button role or activation.

## iOS · Other / native

### MAUI-specific advice on a physical iPhone needs the MAUI option

`maui-ios-detection` · Limitation · FixExamples

- **What:** Scanning and findings work for any app, however it was installed; framework detection only affects fix advice. Swipewalk recognizes .NET MAUI and its Microsoft.Maui.Controls version by reading the app's files, which it can do on the iOS Simulator and on a physical iPhone when Swipewalk installed the app itself (--install <.app/.ipa>), but not for an app already on a physical iPhone (installed through Xcode, TestFlight, the App Store or an MDM). For those, choose ".NET MAUI" as the App framework under More checks on the desktop app's New scan page, or pass --framework maui, to get MAUI fix examples. The Microsoft.Maui.Controls version stays unknown either way, so version-specific hints (for example about live text-size updates, fixed in 10.0.100) ask you to check it yourself.
- **Impact:** Without the MAUI option or flag, fix examples for a MAUI app on a physical iPhone Swipewalk didn't install are in Swift rather than MAUI XAML, the report can't show a Microsoft.Maui.Controls version or apply version-specific advice, and text-size findings leave out their .NET MAUI likely causes. Which findings are raised, and their WCAG mapping, is unaffected.
- **Check manually:** If the app uses .NET MAUI, choose ".NET MAUI" as the App framework under More checks in the desktop app, or pass --framework maui, and check the app's Microsoft.Maui.Controls version yourself against 10.0.100 (see "How .NET MAUI apps apply text-size changes").

## All platforms · .NET MAUI

### MAUI AutomationId is never announced

`maui-automationid-not-announced` · Framework note · ScreenReader

- **What:** AutomationId becomes the Android resource id and the iOS accessibilityIdentifier. Screen readers do not read it, so a control with only an AutomationId has no name.
- **Impact:** Controls that rely on AutomationId are reported as missing a name.
- **Check manually:** Use SemanticProperties.Description for the spoken name and keep AutomationId for tests.

### How .NET MAUI apps apply text-size changes

`maui-ios-text-size-restart` · Framework note · Detection · rules: `text-resize-live`

- **What:** On iOS, Microsoft.Maui.Controls before 10.0.100 does not update text while the app keeps running after the system text size changes, only after the app is terminated and relaunched; this was fixed in 10.0.100 by dotnet/maui#34445 (merged 2026-06-23). Swipewalk reads the Microsoft.Maui.Controls version on the iOS Simulator, and on a physical iPhone when the app is installed with --install <.app/.ipa>. Otherwise the version is unknown and the report says so. The older issues describing the same symptom (dotnet/maui#16625, #11832) are still open as of 2026-09-22 but predate the fix. In our tests (Microsoft.Maui.Controls 10.0.60 and 10.0.101, iOS 26.5 Simulator), Shell tab bar titles did not grow with the text size in either version, live or after a restart; the text-resize check reports that as text that did not scale, which is expected on both tested versions, not a Swipewalk error. On Android, the default MainActivity has no FontScale in ConfigurationChanges, so a font-scale change restarts the activity (returning to its first page) instead of updating text in place; adding ConfigChanges.FontScale avoids the restart, but then text keeps its old size until the app is relaunched unless the app re-applies fonts itself. Separately, `dotnet new maui` with SDK 10.0.300 resolved Microsoft.Maui.Controls 10.0.20 (before the fix) by default, so a new project needs `<MauiVersion>` set explicitly to get 10.0.100 or later.
- **Impact:** People who change text size mid-task see the old size until they restart the app (iOS, and Android when FontScale is handled) or lose their place (Android's default behavior). Shell tab titles may be listed as not resizing even in apps on a fixed MAUI version. record and scan --large-text report the restart-only case as one screen-level platform advisory once the restart is confirmed to show the same screen.
- **Check manually:** Change the text size while the app is running and check whether it takes effect without a restart; if not, relaunch and check text at the new size for clipping. Check the app's Microsoft.Maui.Controls version against 10.0.100.

### MAUI may enlarge small ImageButtons at runtime

`maui-imagebutton-touch-area` · Framework note · Rules · rules: `target-size`

- **What:** An ImageButton declared 20×20 was measured 44×44 on screen on both Android and iOS, because the button is enlarged at runtime. The scanner uses the measured size, not the declared one.
- **Impact:** Sizes in results can differ from WidthRequest/HeightRequest in XAML. The scanner uses the accessibility frame, which is usually but not always the area that responds to touch.
- **Check manually:** Where the XAML size is below 24×24, tap near the edge of the reported area to confirm the enlarged area actually responds.

### Source mapping (--source) for .NET MAUI mostly points at a best guess, not an exact line

`maui-source-mapping-scope` · Limitation · SourceMapping

- **What:** With --source <path>, a finding can carry a source location: the element's own AutomationId, then its literal text in XAML or code-behind, then a .resx string resource, in that order, with an ambiguous match settled by which file shares the most of the screen's other finding labels (reported as "likely", a best guess at the file, never "exact") or left as several candidates when nothing stands out. A hand review of three real .NET MAUI sample apps' source (not written for scanning) found none used AutomationId at all, so identifier matching is expected to rarely fire in practice; the mapper itself has so far been tested only against Swipewalk's own sample app (BuggyApp), not against those real apps. A real app's static screens (toolbars, settings, forms) are expected to resolve well this way, but a list or grid bound to data -- an ordinary, common screen shape -- mostly cannot: a finding whose text comes from bound/computed data with no literal anywhere in the source is reported as "not found", not guessed; only an element with no accessible name at all is tried by size, an adjacent label, or its position inside a repeating template, which gives "likely" (a best guess at the line, never the exact runtime text) or "candidates" (more than one plausible line, none picked). A hand-built custom control with no name of any kind, a framework-injected control (for example MAUI Shell's own flyout menu button), or a control from a NuGet package has no line in the app's own project to point at, and is reported as not found rather than guessed. C# Markup UI is matched only by AutomationId or literal text, never by the size/label/template fallback (it has no XAML tree to walk). This mapper runs only when the screen is detected as MAUI (on a physical iPhone that needs --install or --framework maui); otherwise the screen goes to its own framework's mapper instead -- a native Android Views or Jetpack Compose screen, or an undetected Android screen, to the Android mapper (see "android-source-mapping-scope"); a native iOS screen detected as UIKit or SwiftUI, or not detected at all, to the native iOS mapper (see "ios-source-mapping-scope"); and a React Native or Flutter screen, on either platform, to its own matcher (see "reactnative-flutter-source-mapping-scope"). Xamarin.Forms, MAUI Blazor Hybrid, NativeScript and a WebView-filling hybrid-web app (Ionic, Capacitor, Cordova) are not mapped at all (the finding simply has no source location).
- **Impact:** On a real app, expect "likely"/"candidates"/"not found" as often as, or more often than, "exact" -- especially on list-heavy screens. Swipewalk never proposes a code change from anything but an exact match, and never from a guess.
- **Check manually:** Search the project for the finding's visible text or role to confirm the line yourself, especially for a "likely" or "candidates" result.
- **Planned:** Other frameworks as demand appears.

## Android · Android Views, Jetpack Compose, Other / native

### Source mapping (--source) for native Android Views and Jetpack Compose mostly points at a best guess, not an exact line

`android-source-mapping-scope` · Limitation · SourceMapping

- **What:** With --source <path>, a finding on a native Android Views or Jetpack Compose screen can carry a source location, matched in the same order as MAUI: the element's own identifier (an android:id resource-id, or -- only when the finding's own runtime element actually carries one -- a Compose testTag literal), then its literal accessible text in layout XML or Kotlin/Java source, then a strings.xml resource, then (Compose only, tried only after text matching finds nothing) the fixed prefix of a testTag("prefix${...}") template shared by a repeated composable, then (for an element with no name at all) its declared size or an adjacent label. Kotlin/Java is read by careful lexical scanning of specific patterns (R.string.x/stringResource(...), text/contentDescription/hint assignments, Compose Text(...)/testTag(...) calls) rather than a real compiler front end, so a coincidental textual match is possible; a Compose call's own argument list is matched by a bounded text window around the call, not a real parse of its parentheses, since Kotlin's nesting makes finding a call's exact end hard without one. Views apps usually give an android:id to every view their code touches (findViewById and view binding need one to reach it), so identifier matching is expected to fire more often than for MAUI or Compose -- not yet measured on a real app. A layout XML attribute that explicitly clears a name (android:contentDescription or android:text set to "@null") is not treated as a name. When Kotlin/Java sets the name later with a string literal or a string resource, that assignment is indexed and a finding with that runtime name can resolve to it; a name built from computed or bound data comes back "not found". When the finding's runtime name is still non-empty after that (a sign the name comes from somewhere other than the cleared attribute, most likely Kotlin/Java code) but text matching found nothing more precise, a match against the cleared id falls back to that layout line as "likely" rather than "exact", hedging that the real name MAY be set in code rather than asserting it; when the runtime name is empty instead (a missing-name finding, meaning nothing overrode the clearing), the id match stays "exact" as usual, since the layout line really is where to add one. Android's own framework ids (android:id/title, android:id/icon, ...) are never trusted as a match at all, whether or not the app's own package is known. Separately, an id whose package names a DIFFERENT app entirely (an embedded WebView, a second process, a misidentified multi-module build) is also never trusted -- checked first against the app's OWN package as actually detected from the run being mapped (the most reliable source: a uiautomator resource-id package is the app's actual installed applicationId -- verified with a real build installed on the Android emulator (not yet on a physical phone; 2026-09-28: NativeAndroid's debug build type given applicationIdSuffix ".debugcheck", so applicationId differed from its Gradle namespace): every app-owned resource-id on its first screen (MainActivity) and its Views screen (ViewsActivity) -- every one not in Android's own android: package -- carried the suffixed applicationId, e.g. org.swipewalk.nativeandroid.debugcheck:id/buttonPay, never the plain namespace org.swipewalk.nativeandroid the source declares), falling back to the project's own applicationId read from build.gradle/build.gradle.kts (or namespace) only when the real scanned package isn't known (an older results.json, or a capture where the app's own id itself couldn't be detected); that source-only fallback reads just the base applicationId/namespace and does not apply a buildType's applicationIdSuffix or a product flavor's override, so for such a build it rejects the app's own ids and reports "not found" rather than a wrong line (confirmed for a single-module app's suffixed debug build type; multi-module and product-flavor projects remain untested). This does NOT catch a library dependency's own ids (for example AppCompat's or Material's): Gradle merges a library's resources into the app's own package at build time, so a library id carries the same package as the app's own ids at runtime and can't be told apart this way -- confirmed from a real captured tree (NativeAndroid's AppCompat action_bar/action_bar_container ids both carry the app's own package); a short name the app happens to share with a library's can still resolve "exact". Compose identifier matching depends entirely on the app opting into Modifier.semantics { testTagsAsResourceId = true } -- a testTag existing in source proves nothing about the runtime tree if that flag isn't set, and Swipewalk only trusts a Compose identifier when the finding's own runtime element already carries a resource-id; for a Compose element, that resource-id is only present when the flag was in effect above it (a Compose screen can also host interop AndroidView views that carry a real android:id independently of this flag). A Compose testTag containing a Kotlin string template (for example "card_${id}") is treated as a per-item template: the longest fixed prefix before the template can resolve to "likely", noting the one line probably produces many runtime elements, never "exact" -- or "candidates" when more than one template shares that same prefix. This mapper has so far been tested only against Swipewalk's own sample app (NativeAndroid, a single Gradle module), not against real third-party or multi-module Android apps; that sample doesn't set testTagsAsResourceId, so Compose testTag and testTag-template matching have been tested only on small made-up projects. A very common or very short label (for example "Done" or "Cancel"; the common words are recognized in English only), and a literal in code that also appears as a localized string value, are never reported as "exact" without an identifier (the result is candidates, or at most "likely" with the reason), and a candidate list from a text or identifier match shows at most 10 places and says how many matched. An identifier found in more than one place (an android:id in more than one layout, android:id="@+id/x" or "@id/x", or a Compose testTag literal used more than once) is listed as candidates, never as one exact line.
- **Impact:** On a Compose screen especially, expect "likely"/"candidates"/"not found" as often as, or more often than, "exact" for anything other than a static resource-backed name. Swipewalk never proposes a code change from anything but an exact match, and never from a guess.
- **Check manually:** Search the project for the finding's visible text, resource-id or testTag to confirm the line yourself, especially for a "likely" or "candidates" result, and always for a Compose finding with no identifier.
- **Planned:** Other frameworks as demand appears.

## iOS · UIKit, SwiftUI, Other / native

### Source mapping (--source) for native iOS covers UIKit and SwiftUI, but several patterns aren't traced

`ios-source-mapping-scope` · Limitation · SourceMapping

- **What:** With --source <path> pointed at a native iOS project, a finding can carry a source location: the element's own accessibilityIdentifier, then its literal text in Swift/Objective-C code (including NSLocalizedString and similar macros, and SwiftUI's own Text/Button/Label/Toggle initializers), then a .strings/.xcstrings catalog entry (value matched back to its key, then to where that key is used in code -- catalog values are matched in the base language only; a scan on a device set to another language won't match them), then -- lower confidence, never "exact" -- a storyboard/XIB's own design-time text (or, rarely, an accessibilityIdentifier set from Interface Builder's own Identity Inspector), since a hand review of real, unrelated apps (not written for scanning) found a storyboard/XIB's text is frequently a decoy a developer left for previewing layout: the shipped text is assigned in code via the outlet's own property, and the mapper matches that code assignment directly rather than tracing which storyboard/XIB outlet wires to which property. Only an unlabeled UIKit element created in code (a missing-name finding, `let x = UIButton(...)`) is tried by declared size or an adjacent UILabel, giving "likely" or "candidates" -- an element laid out in a storyboard/XIB is not matched this way, and SwiftUI has no equivalent structural fallback at all, since its views are rarely named local variables. Structural matching searches the WHOLE given source by the element's role, not just the current screen (the same characteristic .NET MAUI's own structural fallback already has); a project with more than one screen that each have their own unlabeled element of the same kind can have one screen's finding point at a DIFFERENT screen's line (confirmed in NativeiOS, which deliberately implements the same screen twice, once in UIKit and once in SwiftUI: the SwiftUI screen's own unlabeled field has no UIKit-shaped declaration of its own to be found, so it resolves to the UIKit screen's field instead of "not found"). A project with two files that plant the identical literal text (also true of NativeiOS, by design, so the two implementations could be compared) resolves as "candidates" listing both files, never a guess between them. A screen whose accessible name comes from a project-specific generated localization API (a SwiftGen-style wrapped accessor, for example) or from a same-file `accessibilityLabel = otherLabel.text` assignment chain is reported as "not found", not traced -- both are real patterns seen in real apps but are a deliberate later phase. A SwiftUI `.accessibilityElement(children: .combine/.contain)` grouping is tried only for a finding whose label looks combined from several views (contains ", ") on a screen that's SwiftUI or has an undetected framework (never a screen confirmed UIKit or MAUI): if the source has exactly one such grouping, it's offered as "likely" the place the name may be assembled -- this is not a proposed literal, and not necessarily this screen's own grouping, since there may be no single line that produces the exact announced text (for example when it's built from several pieces plus live data); with more than one grouping in the source, the result is "not found" rather than a guess. XCUITest itself gives no `traits` field (only a coarse element type, label and identifier), so a "wrong role"/"missing trait" finding has less for the mapper to work from than a MAUI or Android finding does. iOS framework detection is unreliable (XCUITest exposes no class-name signal), so mapping is attempted for any iOS screen detected as UIKit or SwiftUI, or not detected at all -- pass --framework uikit or --framework swiftui explicitly when it stays Unknown and you know which it is. A React Native or Flutter iOS screen goes to its own matcher instead, on either platform (see "reactnative-flutter-source-mapping-scope"); a hybrid-web iOS screen isn't mapped at all. The mapper has been tested against Swipewalk's own sample app (NativeiOS), not a real published app. A very common or very short label (for example "Done" or "Cancel"; the common words are recognized in English only), and a literal in code that also appears as a localized string value, are never reported as "exact" without an identifier (the result is candidates, or at most "likely" with the reason), and a candidate list from a text or identifier match shows at most 10 places and says how many matched. A string defined as a Type.member accessor (for example static let title = NSLocalizedString(...)) is followed to the code that uses it as Type.member; when no such use is found (other ways of referring to it are not followed) the result says it points at the definition.
- **Impact:** Expect "likely"/"candidates"/"not found" often, the same caveat as .NET MAUI. A storyboard/XIB's own design-time text should never be assumed current without checking the code line the mapper points at instead.
- **Check manually:** Search the project for the finding's visible text to confirm the line yourself, especially for a "likely" or "candidates" result, and always check code before trusting a storyboard/XIB's own text.
- **Planned:** Generated localization APIs, assignment-chain tracing, and a SwiftUI structural fallback, as demand appears.

## All platforms · React Native, Flutter

### Source mapping (--source) for React Native and Flutter is lexical, not a real parser, and mostly points at a best guess

`reactnative-flutter-source-mapping-scope` · Limitation · SourceMapping

- **What:** With --source <path>, React Native and Flutter findings can also carry a source location (0.4), on either Android or iOS -- these two mappers run for a screen detected as React Native or Flutter regardless of platform, ahead of the native Android/iOS mappers, which are gated to their own frameworks and never claim a React Native/Flutter screen. Both are read with regex/lexical scanning of the raw .js/.jsx/.ts/.tsx or .dart files, never a real TypeScript or Dart parser -- a literal built from string concatenation, a spread prop, a computed property name, or any other construct these patterns don't recognize is simply not indexed, not guessed at. React Native matches, in order: the element's own testID as a literal, then as the fixed literal prefix of a dynamic per-row testID built with a template literal (e.g. testID={`feedItem-by-${id}`} -- the runtime value can never be predicted from source, so this is reported "likely", never "exact"; a prefix shorter than 3 characters is not indexed as an anchor at all), then a literal accessibilityLabel or plain JSX <Text> text, then a translation key: every "key": "value" string pair in any .json file under the source folder (except package.json, package-lock.json, tsconfig.json and app.json) counts as a possible translation, at any nesting depth and by its own key name only -- so a non-translation JSON file (mock data, a native asset manifest) can produce a "likely" pointer to the wrong file, and a nested TypeScript i18n module or a gettext .po file (both real formats seen in real apps) are out of scope and simply not indexed. Flutter matches, in order: Semantics(identifier: ...), then a literal Text('...'), Semantics(label: ...) or Tooltip(message: ...), then a flat .arb translation key, read the same lexical, any-depth way. Neither framework's translation-key match is ever reported "exact", even when only one use site is found: the "used from" site is any call/reference naming that key found anywhere in the file (React Native: t()/translate()/{id:}; Flutter: a ".keyName" member access on anything) -- a real match, but a looser filter than a literal string match, unlike MAUI's own .resx technique, which also checks the resource class name before the dot. A Flutter widget Key/ValueKey/ObjectKey is deliberately never treated as an identifier or a name: it identifies a widget to Flutter itself (and to Flutter's own test finders such as find.byKey), but is never passed to the platform accessibility tree, so TalkBack/VoiceOver never see it either; a finding that happens to match one is reported not found, with a reason explaining the likely mix-up rather than a silent guess. Neither mapper has MAUI's structural fallback (matching an unnamed element by size, an adjacent label, or its position in a template): an element with no identifier and no name at all is always reported not found here, never a best-guess line. Both walkers skip common build/dependency/VCS folders (bin, obj, node_modules, build, dist, .git, .dart_tool, .pub-cache, .expo, .gradle, coverage, Pods). Both mappers have so far been tested only against small, hand-written synthetic test projects, not a real React Native or Flutter app. A very common or very short label (for example "Done" or "Cancel"; the common words are recognized in English only), and a literal in code that also appears as a localized string value, are never reported as "exact" without an identifier (the result is candidates, or at most "likely" with the reason), and a candidate list from a text or identifier match shows at most 10 places and says how many matched. When the same translation key is in several language files, the text from a file whose name marks it as English (for example en.json, app_en.arb) is used for the key's value and definition line; English in a folder name (en/translation.json) isn't recognized. Flutter also indexes literal tooltip:, semanticLabel: and semanticsLabel: arguments (text with $ interpolation is skipped).
- **Impact:** Expect "not found" more often than MAUI's own mapper gets, especially for an unnamed element and for text built any way other than a plain string literal or a simple template-literal prefix. A translation-key match is always "likely" here, never "exact", and can occasionally point at the wrong JSON/.arb file or the wrong Dart property of the same name. Swipewalk never proposes a code change from anything but an exact match, and never from a guess.
- **Check manually:** Search the project for the finding's visible text, testID/Semantics identifier, or role to confirm the line yourself, especially for a "likely" or "candidates" result -- and always for a translation-key match, since its "used from" site is a weaker filter than MAUI's own.
- **Planned:** A real TypeScript/Dart parser if this proves too imprecise on real apps; other frameworks as demand appears.

## All platforms · Android Views, Jetpack Compose, UIKit, SwiftUI, Flutter, React Native, Hybrid web (WebView)

### Framework-specific fix examples are written from documentation

`framework-specific-fix-examples-unverified` · Limitation · FixExamples

- **What:** Fix examples exist for .NET MAUI, native Android Views, Jetpack Compose, UIKit, SwiftUI, Flutter, React Native and a WebView-filling hybrid-web app (for example Ionic, Capacitor or Cordova); each is written from official documentation -- the framework's own, the W3C/MDN/WebKit/Android references for web content in a WebView, or the library a fix relies on (for example React Navigation) -- and the documentation each example was written from is not shown in the report. The Kotlin and Swift code examples for Android Views, Jetpack Compose, UIKit and SwiftUI were compile-checked; XML/manifest fragments and the Flutter, React Native and hybrid-web examples were not. None of the Android Views, Jetpack Compose, UIKit, SwiftUI, Flutter, React Native or hybrid-web examples has yet been applied in a real app of that framework and rescanned. A framework's own example shows when detection names it -- a Likely detection is labelled "if this app uses X" -- or when --framework names it.
- **Impact:** A framework-specific example may not compile as written, or may already be out of date with that framework's current API, without having been proven by building and running it in a real app of that framework.
- **Check manually:** Check the example compiles against your project's current dependency versions, and confirm the fix actually works by rescanning after applying it.
- **Planned:** Apply each framework's examples in a real app of that framework and rescan to confirm; extend compile-checking to Flutter and React Native when a toolchain is available.
